**Summary.** This work develops optimal strategies for shadow tomography by mapping the required measurement resources onto graph parameters derived from Pauli observables. It establishes theoretical bounds on sample complexity using concepts like fractional chromatic number and provides constructive methods for estimating molecular Hamiltonians with improved variance estimates.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous mathematical tools (graph theory, SDP) to quantify resource requirements for quantum state characterization, directly impacting how we design measurements for near-term quantum hardware.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses shadow tomography: efficiently estimating many expectation values of an unknown quantum state from randomized measurements using a limited number of copies.

**Main result.** It establishes that the required sample complexity parameter is governed by graph parameters of the Pauli anticommutation frustration graph, and shows Clifford measurements can be optimal under certain conditions.

**Method.** The problem is reduced to analyzing graph theory invariants (like fractional chromatic number) associated with the frustration graph, utilizing Semidefinite Programming (SDP) hierarchies for computation.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on Pauli observables $\{S_i\}$ acting on $n$ qubits. The setting considers memoryless protocols and measurements restricted to local subsets of qubits (block-limited).

**Key observables.** Expectation values $	ext{tr}(S_iho)$ for a set of Pauli observables $S=\{S_1, \dots, S_v\}$, and the variance of an estimator $	ext{Var}(\hat{H})$ for Hamiltonian energy estimation.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The sample complexity parameter $\delta(\{S_i\})$, which is bounded by graph parameters like $1/\chi_f(G)$ and $1/\vartheta(ar{G})$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes memoryless measurements and explores the optimality of Clifford measurements, though general cases may require SDP hierarchies.

**Figures summary.** Table II numerically compares variance bounds for Hamiltonian estimation using various measurement strategies (e.g., single-qubit vs. two-qubit Clifford measurements) across different molecules.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theoretical framework by relating tomography efficiency to graph parameters, derives lower and upper bounds on the sample complexity parameter $\delta$, and applies this framework constructively to estimate molecular Hamiltonian energies with improved variance bounds.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Shadow tomography addresses the task of efficiently predicting many expectation values of an unknown quantum state from randomized measurements on comparatively few copies. Existing analyses promise large scaling advantages, but the optimal strategies realizing these guarantees are not always known, and the required measurements are potentially challenging to implement on current hardware. We address this gap for Pauli observables by computing optimal sample-complexity parameters and constructing optimal measurement strategies under realistic resource constraints. We focus on memoryless protocols, where each copy is measured only once, and on measurements with bounded interaction range. Our approach reduces the problem to the analysis of graph parameters of the frustration graph encoding the Pauli anticommutation relations. We provide efficient numerical methods for the general case and analytically prove that Clifford measurements are optimal in many situations. This includes all perfect graphs, all single-qubit, all two-qubit measurement scenarios, and more. Applied to Hamiltonian energy estimation, our framework yields constructive strategies and improved variance bounds for molecular benchmarks.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper provides a detailed theoretical analysis of the secret key rate for QKD over satellite links, specifically addressing the failure of existing security proofs when detector efficiencies mismatch significantly. By employing advanced information theoretic techniques and adapting the decoy-state method, the authors derive more precise bounds necessary for assessing practical quantum communication security.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it tackles a critical practical limitation (detector mismatch) in quantum communication theory, providing necessary theoretical tools for assessing real-world quantum network security.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of accurately estimating the secret key rate for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) when significant detection-efficiency mismatch occurs in realistic satellite communication setups.

**Main result.** The authors develop a rigorous framework to estimate the key rate under large mismatches, showing that existing proofs fail and providing updated bounds based on information theory optimization techniques.

**Method.** The analysis employs Positive Operator-Valued Measures (POVMs) and adapts the decoy-state method within the BB84 protocol framework. Key rates are derived by solving complex optimization problems involving conditional entropies.

**Model / system.** The model simulates a satellite-to-ground QKD link, specifically between the Micius satellite and the Zvenigorod ground station. It utilizes the BB84 protocol considering single-photon states and weak coherent pulses.

**Key observables.** Secret key rate ($K$), conditional von-Neumann entropies, Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), and detection efficiencies ($\eta_{a,\alpha}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Detection-efficiency mismatch magnitude, probability of passing ($p_{	ext{pass}}$), and the average photon number ($\mu$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes an asymptotic limit ($N ightarrow \infty$) and that Eve knows the exact detection efficiency values but cannot manipulate them.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in detail, but references Table I (QKD parameters/Micius) and Table II (atmospheric conditions/detector efficiencies).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from general security proofs to specific estimations using POVMs and decoy states. It presents multiple key rate bounds derived through optimization over symmetry-enforcing linear maps, culminating in an estimate applicable to the Micius satellite link.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Detection-efficiency mismatch is a common problem in realistic quantum key distribution (QKD) systems. The existing security proofs for the case of the passive basis choice provide a nonzero secret key rate only for a small detection-efficiency mismatch. Unfortunately, in realistic setups, the detection-efficiency mismatch can be significant. Here we present a more precise estimation of the secret key rate for the BB84 protocol with the passive basis choice, which accounts for the detection-efficiency mismatch between four threshold detectors as well as an adaptation of the decoy-state method. The suggested approach is used to estimate the secret key rate in a QKD experiment between the Micius satellite and the Zvenigorod ground station.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a formal comparison between different mathematical logics used to model event structures arising from partitions. It distinguishes between algebraic operations like meet and join when combining contexts, showing that simple structural unions often fail to preserve the required logical properties. This has implications for understanding contextuality in both classical set theory and quantum measurement frameworks.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a deep logical foundation for understanding how quantum measurements (modeled by DSDs) relate to classical set theory structures, which is crucial for foundational work in quantum information.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to rigorously distinguish between different mathematical interpretations of 'partition logic' when modeling event structures derived from set partitions.

**Main result.** It shows that the algebraic meet ($\wedge$) captures common coarse-grained events, while the join ($\vee$) requires a Boolean closure that often fails to correspond to a single partition operation, highlighting structural differences between contexts.

**Method.** The analysis uses formal logic structures, comparing Ore's correspondence (mapping partitions to Boolean algebras) with Ellerman's framework involving refinement and direct-sum decompositions (DSDs).

**Model / system.** The model involves event algebras derived from set partitions ($\pi$) of a finite universe $U$, which are used to formalize propositions in quantum or classical measurement contexts.

**Key observables.** Common event algebra (captured by meet $\wedge$), Boolean closure (captured by join $\vee$), and the existence/consistency of context-consistent valuations on DSD projections.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The size of the universe $|U|$, and the specific structure of the generating partitions $\{\pi_k\}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** It assumes that physical contexts can be modeled by set partitions, but notes that the resulting pasted structures are generally not Boolean algebras themselves.

**Figures summary.** Not specified (analysis based on abstract mathematical identities and structural comparisons).

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by defining two distinct uses of 'partition logic,' comparing Ore's correspondence for event algebras with Ellerman's framework using direct-sum decompositions, and analyzing the algebraic consequences of context combination (meet vs. join).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The term ``partition logic'' denotes two constructions at different levels. In automaton and generalized-urn models, selected partitions generate Boolean event algebras whose contextwise union forms a concrete pasted event structure; in Ellerman's framework, whole partitions are classifications governed by refinement and partition operations. For a finite set $U$, Ore's correspondence maps each generator $π$ to its Boolean algebra $\BA(π)$, but it neither identifies the pasted carrier with $\Part(U)$ nor makes pasting a partition operation. It yields $\BA(π\wedgeσ)=\BA(π)\cap\BA(σ)$ and $\BA(π\veeσ)=\langle\BA(π)\cup\BA(σ)\rangle_{\rm BA}$, where $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\rm BA}$ denotes Boolean-algebra generation. Thus meet captures the common event algebra, whereas join gives the ambient Boolean closure. Chinese-lantern, Firefly, and triangular examples distinguish shared events, atomic intertwining, and inherited concrete order. Ellerman's direct-sum decompositions (DSDs) provide a vector-space analogue: component projections of an orthogonal DSD resolve the identity and encode exclusive outcomes, but its components are not equivalence classes of vectors. Gleason and Kochen--Specker applications require globally context-consistent valuations on those projections.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper develops and tests a nanomagnetic reservoir computer using heterogeneous magnetic nanorings. By reading out signals from multiple channels corresponding to different ring widths, the authors show that geometric disorder enhances the system's computational capacity for tasks like time-series prediction. This suggests a scalable route toward magnetic neuromorphic computing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work demonstrates a concrete pathway for integrating concepts from condensed matter physics (magnetic domain dynamics in metamaterials) directly into computational hardware architectures, providing an experimental realization of physical computation principles relevant to open quantum systems modeling.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The research aims to utilize the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of physical magnetic systems for machine learning tasks, specifically reservoir computing, minimizing external training overhead.

**Main result.** Combining outputs from multiple geometrically heterogeneous channels significantly enhances the reservoir's expressivity and computational performance compared to single-channel readouts.

**Method.** The authors tested the system on nonlinear signal transformation (SigT) and Mackey-Glass time-series prediction (MG-TSP) using multi-channel planar Hall effect readout combined with Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

**Model / system.** The platform is a nanomagnetic reservoir computer built from an array of interconnected magnetic nanorings whose track widths are systematically varied across the device. The dynamics are governed by domain-wall motion modulated by a rotating external magnetic field.

**Key observables.** Normalized Root-Mean-Square Error (NRMSE) for prediction tasks, explained variance ratio from PCA, and PHE signals measured at $1f$ and $2f$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Ring track widths ranging from 500 nm to 300 nm; input modulation fields ($H_0$, $H_r$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The improvements in performance are attributed to genuinely diverse feature sets provided by multiple channels, rather than just an increase in trainable parameters.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the pipeline (Input $ightarrow$ Field $ightarrow$ Dynamics $ightarrow$ Output), benchmark task results (SigT/MG-TSP NRMSE heatmaps and plots), and PCA analysis showing explained variance vs. number of components for various channel combinations.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical basis (nanomagnetic reservoir) and then systematically evaluates its performance on two distinct ML tasks, using multi-channel readout and dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA) to quantify the benefit of geometric heterogeneity.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Physical reservoir computing utilizes the intrinsic nonlinear and history-dependent dynamics of physical systems to perform machine-learning tasks with minimal training overhead. Here, we introduce a nanomagnetic reservoir computer based on a heterogeneous array of interconnected magnetic nanorings, combined with multi-channel planar Hall effect readout. The device comprises subarrays of rings with systematically varied track widths ranging from 500 nm to 300 nm, enabling access to the heterogeneous dynamics of geometrically diverse magnetic systems within a single reservoir. By applying time-varying input signals as modulations of a driving rotating magnetic field, we evaluate the nanoring reservoir's performance on nonlinear signal transformation and Mackey-Glass time-series prediction tasks. We find that combining outputs from multiple width-dependent channels significantly reduces the normalized root-mean-square error compared to single-channel readout, with the optimal channel combinations depending on task requirements. These results demonstrate that geometric heterogeneity provides an additional, experimentally accessible degree of freedom and complementary computational features. Principal component analysis further reveals that a reduced subset of correlated features captures most of the computationally relevant information while suppressing noise contributions. These results demonstrate that controlled geometric heterogeneity enhances reservoir expressivity and suggest a route toward scalable magnetic computing architectures in which multi-output magnetic metamaterials serve as configurable dynamical building blocks for device networks.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper explores localization in interacting, non-Hermitian quasiperiodic systems, establishing that the binding configuration of particles dictates their transport properties. By analyzing effective Hamiltonians, the authors show a controllable 'localization inversion' where composite pairs remain extended even when individual unpaired particles become localized. This highlights internal interactions as a powerful control mechanism beyond external potentials.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a detailed theoretical framework showing how emergent collective behavior (the composite state) can decouple its transport properties from the single-particle physics dictated by external disorder or non-Hermiticity.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates whether composite excitations can exhibit localization behavior opposite to their constituent particles within a non-Hermitian quasiperiodic environment.

**Main result.** The paper demonstrates that internal particle configuration acts as a reversible control parameter, allowing for controllable localization inversion where the composite state remains extended while unpaired constituents localize.

**Method.** The analysis uses effective Hamiltonian derivations via perturbation theory and diagnoses localization using the Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) across varying system sizes.

**Model / system.** The model is an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder hosting hard-core bosons, governed by a complex potential $V(\Delta\phi)$ and interaction terms $H_{	ext{int}}$.

**Key observables.** Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR) for localization diagnosis; particle density profiles ($\langle n_{eta,j} angle$); effective pair hopping ($J_{eff,j}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Non-Hermiticity strength ($h$); relative phase $\Delta\phi$; interaction strength $U_1$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the strongly interacting regime ($U_1 \gg |J|, |t|, |V|$) and assumes quasi-degeneracy for perturbation theory application.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate IPR evolution showing distinct localization paths for paired vs. unpaired states, confirming the persistence of an extended composite band embedded within a localized continuum across increasing system sizes.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from analyzing the basic antisymmetric case ($\Delta\phi=0$) to deriving effective Hamiltonians for the pair sector using perturbation theory, culminating in demonstrating configuration-dependent localization inversion and stabilizing extended states via engineered interactions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

A composite excitation need not inherit the localization behavior of its constituents. We show that an interacting non-Hermitian quasiperiodic ladder realizes a controllable and reversible localization inversion between composite and unbound excitations, where internal configuration, rather than only the external potential, becomes a control parameter for localization. Opposite complex potentials on the two legs cancel at first order for a same-rung pair but act directly on separated particles, allowing extended composite states to persist while the unpaired sector becomes localized. A strong-coupling theory identifies the composite state as an emergent weakly modulated non-Hermitian quasicrystal generated by virtual unpaired configurations. Breaking the potential antisymmetry restores a direct modulation of the composite band and reverses the localization hierarchy. Engineering configuration-space pathways further stabilizes an extended composite band embedded within a localized continuum, the inverse of the conventional bound-state-in-the-continuum scenario. Our results establish internal configuration as a reversible control parameter for localization.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper uses advanced CFT techniques to analyze how generalized symmetries stabilize massless Renormalization Group flows between minimal models. It demonstrates that specific unbroken symmetries eliminate dangerous perturbations, confirming the stability of the resulting infrared phase as a gapless state. This work provides a deep connection between abstract algebraic structures and the robustness of physical quantum phases.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of symmetry enforcing stability in RG flows is highly relevant for understanding quantum critical points and topological order in condensed matter systems, providing a powerful theoretical tool beyond standard perturbation theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how generalized symmetry dictates the stability of massless Renormalization Group (RG) flows or Higgs transitions between different Conformal Field Theories (CFTs). The core goal is to understand how unbroken symmetries enforce gapless phases during these theoretical phase changes.

**Main result.** In specific minimal model flows, the presence of an unbroken fusion ring symmetry eliminates all relevant perturbations in the infrared theory, confirming its stability as a (weak-)symmetry-enforced gapless phase. Furthermore, this structure dictates potential cascade effects between different fixed points.

**Method.** The analysis employs Hamiltonian formalism for CFTs and their RG mappings, combining perturbative checks with nonperturbative algebraic methods involving symmetry constraints like fusion rings and coset structures.

**Model / system.** The primary system is the massless RG flow between unitary minimal models, specifically $M(p, p+1) ightarrow M(p-1, p)$, which models theoretical phase transitions analogous to Higgs phenomena. The underlying mathematical framework involves CFTs and their associated symmetry algebras.

**Key observables.** Unbroken fusion ring symmetry $	ext{FR}(SU(2)_{p-2})$, stability of the infrared (IR) fixed point, and the structure of (half-)integer spin nonsimple currents.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The integer parameter $p$ defining the minimal models ($p>3$), and the flow parameters governing relevant/irrelevant perturbations.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the existence of RG flows and relies heavily on symmetry arguments to prove stability, contrasting with purely algebraic methods that might not guarantee physical stability.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 summarizes key concepts: pairing structure involving nonsimple currents, symmetry-enforced gaplessness, coset/level rank duality structures, and the potential for phase transition cascades.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the RG flow by first establishing the role of generalized symmetry in stabilizing the IR theory. It then details how specific symmetries (like $	ext{FR}(SU(2)_{p-2})$) eliminate relevant perturbations, leading to conclusions about gapless phases and potential cascade dynamics.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the role of generalized symmetry in massless renormalization group flows or Higgs transitions. In particular, we revisit the massless renormalization group flows in unitary minimal models, $\mathbf{M}(p,p+1) \rightarrow \overline{\mathbf{M}(p-1,p)}$ preserving the fusion ring symmetry $\text{FR} (SU(2)_{p-2})\subset \mathbf{M}(p,p+1)$ where $p$ is an integer satisfying $p>3$. In this series of flows, we demonstrate that the unbroken fusion ring symmetry $\text{FR} (SU(2)_{p-2})$ eliminates all relevant perturbations in the $\overline{\mathbf{M}(p-1,p)}$ model. Hence, the infrared theory $\overline{\mathbf{M}(p-1,p)}$ is stable at the level of the scaling analysis and can be interpreted as a (weak-)symmetry-enforced gapless phase in contemporary theoretical physics. Phenomenologically, by the folding trick, the unbroken fusion ring symmetry corresponds to a (half-)integer spin nonsimple current, a variant of the Cooper pair involving nonabelian anyons generated from the coset or level-rank duality structures. Moreover, we demonstrate that the structure of (half-)integer spin nonsimple current plays a fundamental role in causing the resonance effect of relevant and dangerously irrelevant perturbations. This resonance effect may result in the cascade of phase transitions (or the system flows to unexplored fixed points), and the symmetry can be a stopper of such unconventional flows.

</details>

**Summary.** This work provides a deep theoretical analysis of physical systems governed by non-split 2-group symmetries. By employing advanced tools from algebraic topology and category theory, the authors classify quantum anomalies and map out the landscape of possible topological and physical boundary phases for (3+1)D TQFTs.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical framework connecting higher-dimensional topological field theories, generalized symmetries (2-groups), and anomaly classification is highly relevant for understanding exotic phases of matter beyond standard Landau theory in condensed matter physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper systematically studies finite, non-split 2-group symmetries with non-trivial Postnikov classes in the context of (3+1)D Topological Quantum Field Theories (TQFTs). It aims to classify associated anomalies and boundary conditions.

**Main result.** The authors classified anomalies by computing oriented and spin bordism groups for low dimensions ($d \le 5$) and identified multiple minimal Lagrangian algebras corresponding to different topological and physical boundary phases.

**Method.** The methodology combines advanced algebraic topology (bordism theory, cohomology) with categorical methods (fusion 2-categories) applied to TQFT formalism. They analyze the structure of weak 2-group symmetries.

**Model / system.** The focus is on physical theories in $d$-dimensional spacetime exhibiting a non-split 2-group symmetry $\mathcal{G}$. The analysis covers both gapped and gapless phases, relating to Symmetry Protected Topological (SPT) phases.

**Key observables.** Anomalies classified by cohomology groups like $H^4(B\mathcal{G}; U(1)) \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$, and the identification of various boundary conditions (e.g., symmetric, partial SSB, G-SPT).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimension of spacetime ($d$), the structure of the 2-group symmetry $\mathcal{G}$, and the non-trivial Postnikov class.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the weak 2-group formulation and may require assuming a twisted spin structure on the underlying manifold for certain calculations.

**Figures summary.** Tables summarize calculated bordism groups (Table 1) and different physical boundary conditions/phases (Table 2). Figures illustrate defect interactions and the physical meaning of the Postnikov class.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by defining the non-split 2-group symmetry, calculating its anomalies using bordism theory for $d \le 5$, then applying this to construct and classify the resulting Symmetry TQFTs ($	ext{SymTFT}$) and their boundary conditions via categorical methods.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We present a systematic study of finite, non-split 2-group symmetries with a non-trivial Postnikov class, focusing on the simplest example with a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ 0-form symmetry and a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ 1-form symmetry, intertwined together by the non-trivial Postnikov class in $H^3(B\mathbb{Z}_2;\mathbb{Z}_2)\cong\mathbb{Z}_2$, denoted by $\mathcal{G}$. We classify the anomalies of this 2-group symmetry for physical theories in $d$-dimensional spacetime, by computing the oriented bordism groups $Ω_{d+1}^{\rm SO}(B\mathcal{G})$ and the spin bordism groups $Ω_{d+1}^{\rm Spin}(B\mathcal{G})$ for $d\leq 5$. For the case of $d=3$, we investigate the Symmetry TFT/TO of the 2-group symmetry $\mathcal{G}$ using the language of fusion 2-categories, as well as (3+1)D TQFT actions, for the cases without or with the 2-group anomaly classified by $\operatorname{Hom}\left(\widetildeΩ_4^{\rm SO}(B\mathcal{G}),U(1)\right) \cong H^4(B\mathcal{G};U(1))\cong\mathbb{Z}_2$. We classify the minimal topological and physical boundary conditions of the Symmetry TFTs, and carry out the categorical Landau paradigm for such non-split finite 2-group.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors engineered a novel quantum sensor by embedding nitrogen-vacancy nanodiamonds onto birefringent biomineral microcarriers. This carrier stabilizes the quantum emitter against liquid motion while providing an active, proton-sensitive interface. The resulting platform enables versatile, multimodal sensing of magnetic fields and chemical species in complex biological media.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges solid-state quantum emitters (NV centers) with complex soft matter interfaces (biomineral carbonates) to create robust, field-deployable sensors. The integration of mechanical stabilization (birefringence) with chemical sensing mechanisms is highly relevant for open quantum systems research.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Liquid nanodiamond quantum sensors are limited by Brownian rotation, variable photon collection, and perturbations from optical trapping, hindering their use as stable probes in complex media.

**Main result.** By assembling NV centers on birefringent biomineral microcarriers, the system achieves orientation stabilization and demonstrates multimodal sensing (magnetic field and proton/pH) with high sensitivity in liquid environments.

**Method.** The authors combine optical trapping, birefringence-induced torque for mechanical stabilization, ODMR spectroscopy for magnetic measurements, and relaxometry ($T_1$) to probe chemical interactions.

**Model / system.** The platform uses 40-nm NV nanodiamonds anchored to porous vaterite microspherulites. The system is modeled using grand canonical charge-regulation models that couple proton chemical potential to interfacial switching kinetics, alongside an effective spin Hamiltonian for optical readout.

**Key observables.** Zeeman-split resonances (magnetic field sensing), $T_1$ relaxation times ($\mu	ext{s}$ scale), and concentration/pH sensitivities ($\mu	ext{M} \cdot 	ext{Hz}^{-1/2}$, $	ext{mPH} \cdot 	ext{Hz}^{-1/2}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Magnetic fields up to $0.8 	ext{ mT}$; proton doses in the range of $10.7 \, \mu	ext{M}$ (DMEM); characteristic relaxation times ($	au_{	ext{match}} \approx 55 	ext{ ps}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The carrier provides an addressable body frame via optical torque, stabilizing the sensor against Brownian motion; chemical sensing relies on modeling the interface as a proton-active thermodynamic boundary.

**Figures summary.** Figures map the sequence from assembly to readout (optical, Zeeman, chemical); structural evidence confirms NV localization at the carrier–liquid interface; and subsequent figures detail polarization dependence and $T_1$ decay curves under varying conditions.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first identifying limitations in free nanodiamonds, then presenting the engineered birefringent carrier platform. It details measurements across magnetic sensing (Zeeman splitting), chemical sensing ($T_1$ in DMEM/ethanol), and concludes with a theoretical model coupling proton chemistry to quantum dynamics.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Mobile nanodiamond quantum sensors in liquids are limited by Brownian rotation, variable photon collection, and perturbations introduced by optical trapping. Here, we assemble 40-nm nitrogen-vacancy nanodiamonds at the surface of porous, birefringent vaterite microspherulites. This carbonate biomineral provides a polarization-addressable body frame, anisotropic emission redistribution, and a proton-active thermodynamic interface. Under 976-nm optical trapping, the hybrids retain their spin resonance and longitudinal relaxation, with the resonance contrast varying by less than 7 percent and the resonance centre shifting by approximately 1 MHz at 0.8 W. Zeeman-split resonances enable magnetic-field sensing from 0 to 0.8 mT, with a response metric of 78-144 microT per square root Hz. In buffered cell-culture medium, a 10.7 microM nominal proton-equivalent dose shortens T1 from 23.4 +/- 2.3 to 9.0 +/- 1.2 microseconds, corresponding to concentration and pH sensitivities of 6.46 microM per square root Hz and 6.54 mpH per square root Hz, respectively, in DMEM. By contrast, a 500-fold higher proton dose in ethanol produces a substantially weaker spin response, highlighting the role of the carbonate-rich interface. We develop a grand-canonical charge-regulation model coupling proton chemical potential to interfacial switching kinetics within the NV spectral window, capturing medium-dependent dynamic proton transduction. By integrating orientation stabilisation, optical manipulation, magnetic sensing, and interfacial chemical response, this carbonate-rich hybrid platform establishes a versatile approach to multimodal quantum sensing in complex biological liquids.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes how the finite lifetime of an observer, modeled by a causal diamond, induces thermal effects on multipartite quantum states. Using advanced entropy measures, the authors find that particle statistics and entanglement structure dictate whether nonseparability degrades or even enhances under these relativistic conditions. The results provide crucial insights for designing quantum information protocols in curved spacetimes.

**Why it may be interesting.** It connects fundamental concepts from general relativity (causal structure, horizons) directly to quantum information measures like entanglement robustness, which is highly relevant for understanding quantum computation in curved spacetime.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how causal restrictions, modeled by a finite-lifetime observer within a causal diamond spacetime, induce thermal effects that alter the nonseparability of multipartite quantum states.

**Main result.** Thermalization can enhance fermionic W state nonseparability (unlike bosons), and GHZ states maintain nonseparability independent of particle number N, while W states show degradation with increasing N.

**Method.** The authors use the Abe-Rajagopal (AR) q-conditional entropy as a diagnostic tool to quantify nonseparability in bosonic and fermionic systems quantized within the causal diamond geometry.

**Model / system.** The system involves N-partite bosonic and fermionic GHZ and W states, analyzed under the influence of a causal diamond horizon which induces an Unruh-like thermal effect.

**Key observables.** Nonseparability quantified by AR q-conditional entropy; particle number distributions (Bose-Einstein/Fermi-Dirac).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Observer lifetime ($T=2\alpha$), the nonextensivity parameter $q$, and the particle number $N$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the initial state is in the global Minkowski vacuum, and the thermalization arises from tracing out inaccessible exterior modes.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the diagrammatic correspondence between Rindler wedges and the causal diamond under conformal mapping.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the physical context (causal diamonds inducing thermalization), details the mathematical tool (AR q-conditional entropy), and applies it to analyze specific states (GHZ/W).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the nonseparability of multipartite bosonic and fermionic $GHZ$ and $W$ states in a causal diamond spacetime using the Abe-Rajagopal (AR) $q$-conditional entropy. The finite lifetime of the observer gives rise to a causal diamond horizon, which induces an Unruh-like thermal effect and leads to a nontrivial restructuring of nonseparability in $N$-partite systems. Our main result is that the thermal effect can enhance a net nonseparability of fermionic $W$ states, in sharp contrast to the general expectation that relativistic thermalization leads to a monotonic degradation of bosonic nonseparability. In addition, we find that fermionic nonseparability is generally more robust than its bosonic counterpart under causal diamond restrictions. Among different entangled resources, $GHZ$ states exhibit stronger nonseparability and greater robustness than $W$ states under identical causal conditions. We further show that the nonseparability of $W$ states decreases with increasing particle number $N$, whereas that of $GHZ$ states remains independent of $N$ in causal diamond spacetime. These results demonstrate that particle statistics, entanglement structure, and observer lifetime jointly determine the persistence of nonseparability in causally restricted spacetimes, providing insights for relativistic quantum information processing.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper addresses the limitation of tight-binding models that fail when calculating properties sensitive to spatial geometry, despite accurately predicting band structures. The authors propose an 'optimally embedded' framework, treating orbital positions as tunable parameters fixed against experimental or ab-initio data. This allows for the construction of highly accurate minimal models capable of reproducing complex geometric observables like optical responses.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on solid-state physics, the methodology—treating geometric structure (embeddings) as tunable model parameters fixed by external data to improve predictive power—is a general concept applicable to parameterizing complex quantum systems where full first-principles calculation is prohibitive.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Tight-binding models fail to accurately reproduce geometry-dependent physical responses, even when they correctly model geometry-independent properties like band structures.

**Main result.** The authors introduce an 'optimally embedded tight binding' framework where orbital embeddings are treated as explicit tuning parameters fixed against reference data to achieve accurate minimal models.

**Method.** They determine optimal embeddings by decomposing observable quantities into geometry-independent and dependent parts, utilizing position derivatives for efficient fitting.

**Model / system.** The study uses solid-state systems modeled via tight-binding theory (e.g., GaAs, CdS), focusing on the Hamiltonian structure derived from Bloch states and incorporating orbital embeddings ($	au_\alpha$).

**Key observables.** Non-linear optical responses ($\sigma(\omega)$), quantum geometric tensor, and local metric trace.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Orbital embedding parameters ($\{	au_\alpha\}$) are the key tunable parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The initial approximation assumes orbitals are nearly point-like; the method requires fixing embeddings against external physical data (ab-initio or experiment).

**Figures summary.** Figures compare optical responses using different embedding models and show that fitting optimal embeddings on a coarse grid successfully reproduces the true, dense response.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the failure of standard tight-binding models for geometry dependence. It then introduces the optimal embedding framework, detailing the mathematical decomposition used to tune parameters against physical observables, culminating in successful quantitative reproduction of optical responses.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In tight-binding models, the position operator is reduced to intra-cell orbital positions (embeddings). While accurately reproducing band structures, such models often fail for geometry dependent responses depending on the position operator. To address this, we investigate the role of these embeddings and introduce the general framework of optimally embedded tight binding. Treating the embeddings as geometric tuning parameters to be fixed against a reference response (obtained from ab-initio computation or experiment), we obtain tight-binding models of GaAs and CdS which quantitatively reproduce non-linear optical responses at no cost to band structure accuracy. The optimal embeddings are determined efficiently using position derivatives obtained from decomposing tight-binding observables into a geometry independent and dependent part, and explicit derivatives are provided for key quantities such as the quantum geometric tensor. The decomposition reveals where geometric effects dominate, and we show in both toy models and in the Chern insulator V2O3 how geometry can dramatically alter the local metric trace. Our results highlight that orbital embeddings should be treated as a genuine model parameter which should be explicitly fixed against physical data to get accurate minimal models.

</details>

### [How to Test Bell Nonlocality for Gravity?](http://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08778v1)

**Authors:** Debarshi Das, Mir Alimuddin, Simon Storz, Yiwen Chu, Sougato Bose  
**Type:** theory · **Category:** other · **PDF:** <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08778v1>  
**Analysis basis:** full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
**Topic relevance:** `QC/QI experiment` **2/5** · `quantum measurements` **2/5** · `analog quantum simulation` **1/5**

**Summary.** This paper outlines a novel, loophole-free experiment to test if the gravitational field exhibits Bell nonlocality. It uses four massive objects placed in spatial superpositions whose spins are entangled and subsequently interact gravitationally. A violation of the CHSH inequality in local spin measurements would provide evidence that gravity itself is fundamentally quantum mechanical.

**Why it may be interesting.** It proposes an experimental roadmap for testing fundamental quantum principles (Bell nonlocality) in a regime where gravity is treated as a quantum field, bridging quantum information theory with general relativity.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to develop a protocol to test Bell nonlocality directly on the gravitational field itself, moving beyond testing entanglement only in the masses or interactions.

**Main result.** The authors propose a loophole-free, fully device-independent test that can certify Bell nonlocality of gravitational curvatures if gravity is quantum mechanical.

**Method.** A multi-step protocol involving creating spatial superpositions on source and probe masses, allowing them to interact gravitationally, and then performing local spin measurements to violate the CHSH inequality.

**Model / system.** The system involves four massive objects ($M_1, M_2$ sources; $M_0, M_3$ probes) with embedded entangled spins. The interaction is mediated by gravity, leading to entanglement of gravitational curvatures.

**Key observables.** Violation of the Bell-CHSH inequality ($B > 2$), and the resulting post-selected correlations in the spin measurements.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The protocol requires specific mass values ($\sim 10^{-13} - 10^{-14}$ kg) and superposition sizes ($\Delta x \sim 1 - 100 \mu$m) to achieve a measurable violation.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Key assumptions include the ability to make electromagnetic interactions negligible, achieving long-distance entanglement distribution (closing locality loopholes), and assuming fair post-selection in the Bell test analysis.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the geometry of two entangled source masses interacting with two probe masses.

**Paper structure.** The paper details a multi-step protocol: entangling spins, creating spatial superpositions via unitary evolution, allowing gravitational interaction between sources and probes, performing local measurements on source spins (Step 5), and finally measuring probe spins to test Bell nonlocality (Step 6).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose an experiment to test Bell nonlocality, a genuine nonclassicality, for the gravitational field. Two masses with embedded entangled spins (e.g., two diamonds with their NV-centre spins entangled) are placed well outside each other's light cones, ensuring a locality-loophole-free scenario. The spins are then coupled to the motion of their respective masses to generate spatial superpositions. Finally, local measurements are performed only on the gravitational fields of the two masses. If gravity is quantum, then the two entangled masses would entangle their gravitational fields, leading to correlations certifying Bell nonlocality of gravity. Trapped and ground-state cooled nano-objects with micron-sized spatial superposition are sufficient for this test. This goes beyond the recent proposals to test nonclassicality of gravity by providing, for the first time in the literature, a minimal tool to (i) create Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) state of gravitational curvatures, (ii) witness entangled gravitational curvatures, (iii) rule out any local-realist description of gravity, and (iv) achieve a loophole-free test of gravity's nonclassicality in a fully device-independent way.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper proposes a magnetic-Doppler nuclear frequency comb memory for storing hard X-ray photons. It overcomes the difficulty of on-demand retrieval by introducing a mechanism that requires synchronously reversing both the internal magnetic field and absorber velocities. This hybrid approach significantly reduces mechanical complexity while maintaining high storage efficiency.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses quantum light storage and retrieval using solid-state systems, which is a major area of research at the intersection of AMO physics and quantum optics. The use of hyperfine structure to simplify mechanical requirements is particularly novel.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is achieving efficient, on-demand retrieval of hard X-ray photons stored in quantum memories.

**Main result.** A hybrid magnetic-Doppler nuclear frequency comb protocol allows for on-demand storage and retrieval by synchronously reversing both the internal magnetic field and absorber velocities.

**Method.** The method involves engineering a time-reversed phase evolution dynamic by controlling two external parameters (magnetic field and velocity) simultaneously, rather than relying solely on mechanical motion.

**Model / system.** The system utilizes nuclear transitions in ${}^{57}	ext{FeBO}_3$ absorbers, forming a hybrid comb structure incorporating both Doppler shifts ($\Delta\omega_D$) from motion and hyperfine splittings ($\Delta\omega_Z$) from the strong internal magnetic field.

**Key observables.** Storage efficiency ($\eta$), fidelity ($F$), bandwidth (e.g., $3\Delta\omega$ or $6\Delta\omega$), and the retrieval amplitude $	ext{B}_{	ext{out}}(t)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The required simultaneous reversal of both hyperfine magnetic fields ($B_{	ext{hf}}$) and absorber velocities ($\mathbf{v}_n$). The efficiency can reach up to 54% under optimal conditions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** On-demand retrieval necessitates the simultaneous reversal of both $B_{	ext{hf}}$ and $\mathbf{v}_n$; partial reversal is insufficient. Quadrupole interaction in ${}^{57}	ext{FeBO}_3$ can be neglected at low temperatures.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare quantum memory efficiencies ($\eta$) and fidelities ($F$) for static vs. on-demand configurations (C-NFC, S-NFC, D-NFC), illustrating the performance gains from active switching.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the limitations of traditional Doppler frequency combs for on-demand retrieval. It then proposes and details the hybrid magnetic-Doppler NFC using ${}^{57}	ext{FeBO}_3$. The core mechanism involves deriving the time-reversed dynamics enabled by simultaneous field/velocity reversal, leading to performance comparisons between different comb configurations (C-NFC vs D-NFC).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Nuclear quantum memories in the hard X-ray regime offer some key advantages over their optical counterparts, such as broader bandwidth and lower background noise. A Doppler frequency comb protocol has been theoretically proposed [X. Zhang \textit{et al.}, Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{123}, 250504 (2019)] and recently demonstrated experimentally [S. Velten \textit{et al.}, Sci. Adv. \textbf{10}, eadn9825 (2024)] for the storage and retrieval of X-ray photons. However, achieving on-demand retrieval remains challenging because of the requirement for precise and synchronous mechanical motion of multiple absorbers. We propose a hybrid, magnetic-Doppler nuclear frequency comb composed of Doppler-shifted resonant absorbers with lifted nuclear spin degeneracy, which expands the Doppler comb structure. By synchronously reversing the directions of both the magnetic fields and absorber velocities, the system achieves time-reversed phase evolution dynamics that allows for efficient on-demand photon retrieval with significantly reduced mechanical complexity.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents QTris, a board game designed as a pedagogical tool to teach Quantum Mechanics at the high-school level. It advocates for teaching QM using a qubit-first approach rather than historical narratives, focusing on core postulates like superposition and measurement. Preliminary testing suggests that this interactive game format is an effective way to build initial conceptual understanding of quantum principles.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on pedagogy, the reliance on simulating quantum processes via qubits directly relates to foundational concepts in quantum information theory and computation that are relevant to AMO research.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is developing an effective, accessible pedagogical tool to teach abstract concepts of Quantum Mechanics (QM) to high-school students.

**Main result.** The paper introduces QTris, a board game that successfully simulates core quantum processes using a qubit-first approach, showing preliminary evidence of its utility in promoting conceptual understanding.

**Method.** The authors combine pedagogical theory (critiquing historical QM teaching) with empirical testing using student performance data from an educational activity based on the game mechanics.

**Model / system.** The model is QTris, a board game designed to simulate quantum processes on a system of qubits, focusing specifically on two-state systems. The underlying physics concepts simulated include superposition, unitary transformations, and probabilistic measurement.

**Key observables.** Student performance scores across conceptual and operational questions (Q1-Q12), measuring understanding of incompatibility and probabilistic outcomes.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The system is restricted to the two-state qubit model for pedagogical simplicity; the activity involved approximately 150 high-school students.

**Assumptions / limitations.** It assumes that restricting QM education to finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces (qubits) is sufficient and pedagogically sound, bypassing advanced mathematics like functional analysis.

**Figures summary.** Figures show score distributions for conceptual vs. operational questions, and specific response distributions highlighting common student misconceptions regarding probabilities and outcomes.

**Paper structure.** The paper first argues for a qubit-first pedagogical approach over historical narratives; it then details the QTris game rules and mechanics; finally, it reports on preliminary results from an educational activity using the game.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this paper we introduce the new version of QTris, a board game designed to teach and learn Quantum Mechanics within the framework of Quantum Information and Computation. The key idea behind the game is that every game sequence simulates a process on a system of qubits. Thus, QTris can be effectively integrated as a pedagogical tool to teach Quantum Mechanics at high-school level following a two-state approach. After arguing in support of this latter approach, we describe QTris' basic rules and some of its possible extensions, emphasizing how the game mechanics puts in clear light key quantum concepts such as incompatibility, probabilistic measurement and unitary transformation. Moreover, we report on the results of a QTris-based educational activity which involved about 150 high-school students and provided encouraging preliminary indications that QTris can be a useful pedagogical platform to promote an immediate understanding of some key concepts of Quantum Mechanics.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper systematically compares three mathematical approaches—PDF fitting, linearization, and CDF fitting—to estimate the non-extensiveness parameter ($q$) characterizing heavy-tailed distributions in complex systems. By testing these methods on diverse data like solar wind and financial returns, the authors demonstrate that the CDF-based method yields more stable results, offering a robust tool for analyzing non-equilibrium physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous comparison of estimation techniques for heavy tails is methodologically valuable. The emphasis on bin-free methods echoes concerns in quantum information theory regarding noise modeling and parameter extraction from noisy measurements.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study addresses analyzing nonlinear, non-equilibrium phenomena characterized by heavy-tailed distributions that require non-extensive statistics.

**Main result.** The analysis suggests that fitting the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) provides a significantly more stable estimate for the non-extensiveness parameter ($q$) compared to direct PDF or linearized methods.

**Method.** A systematic comparison of three estimation techniques—direct nonlinear PDF fitting, q-logarithm linearization, and numerical CDF fitting—is employed across diverse datasets.

**Model / system.** The analysis utilizes the q-Gaussian distribution, which is appropriate for systems exhibiting long-range correlations beyond standard Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics. Data sources include solar wind proton density, Bitcoin returns, and river discharge data.

**Key observables.** The non-extensiveness parameter ($q$), fit quality metrics like $R^2$, and the estimated parameters $a$ and $b$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The entropic index $q$; sensitivity to histogram binning (number of bins).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that non-extensive statistics are appropriate for describing the observed fluctuations; a major limitation noted is the inherent subjectivity and noise associated with histogram binning.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare $q$-Gaussian vs. Gaussian fits across three datasets (solar wind, Bitcoin, river discharge). Crucially, figures plot estimated $q$ versus the number of histogram bins for all three methods, highlighting method divergence.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the need for non-extensive statistics, details the mathematical framework and three distinct fitting methodologies, applies these methods to multiple real-world datasets (geophysics, finance, hydrology), compares the results systematically, and concludes by advocating for the stability of the CDF approach.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Nature exhibits a wide variety of nonlinear phenomena characterized by strong fluctuations that push the system away from equilibrium. Recent studies have shown that non-extensive statistics are more suitable for analyzing these phenomena, as they can capture long-range correlations and heavy-tailed distributions that conventional Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics cannot represent. However, estimating the non-extensiveness parameter ($q$) is not trivial, and methods vary significantly across disciplines.   This paper presents a systematic and interdisciplinary comparison of three fitting methods: direct nonlinear fitting of the probability distribution function (PDF), linearization using the q-logarithm function, and numerical fitting of the cumulative distribution function (CDF). We applied this analysis to various phenomena, from areas such as geophysics, space weather and economics, analyzing the critical impact of discretization. The results show that $q$ estimates are highly sensitive to histogram binning, while the CDF-based method provides a bin-free alternative that yields more stable estimates for the datasets analyzed here. This contribution provides relevant information for the search for a method that allows the correct determination of the parameters of heavy-tailed distributions in various disciplines.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical work unifies information propagation and learning theory for infinitely wide, deep neural networks. It identifies a critical parameter regime where gradient flow is sustained to infinite depth. The key finding is the direct mathematical equivalence between the network's asymptotic correlation structure and its governing Neural Tangent Kernel.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on deep learning, the mathematical machinery—analyzing spectral properties of large random matrices (Jacobian/NTK) in infinite limits—shares strong conceptual links with analyzing dynamics in complex disordered systems or spin-glass models.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to establish a unified theoretical framework connecting information/gradient propagation properties of deep neural networks to their learning dynamics.

**Main result.** It proves that correlation propagation to infinite depth is only possible at a critical point, where the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) becomes exactly proportional to the output correlation at infinite depth.

**Method.** The analysis combines mean-field theory and random matrix theory to derive recursive relations for network correlations and Jacobians in the limit of infinitely wide and deep networks.

**Model / system.** The model is a deep neural network ($\Psi_	heta$) analyzed in the infinite-width (mean-field) and infinite-depth limits. The analysis focuses on how information propagates through layers governed by weight matrices and activation functions.

**Key observables.** End-to-end Jacobian, Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), output correlation matrix ($\Theta^L$), and their respective second moments.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The critical point in the weight-bias variance plane; infinite width ($N 	o \infty$) and infinite depth ($L 	o \infty$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes specific moment concentration properties (e.g., empirical moments converge to ensemble averages) and relies on mild assumptions about the activation function.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first defining the problem in terms of information flow and learning dynamics, deriving recursive relations for correlations and Jacobians using mean-field theory, identifying the critical regime where propagation is possible, and finally proving the equivalence between NTK and correlation at this critical point.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The initialisation of deep neural networks determines whether information and gradients can propagate across depth, yet a unified theory connecting these properties to learning dynamics remains elusive. Combining mean-field theory and random matrix theory, we establish a direct link between correlation propagation and the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) that governs learning in the sequential limit of infinitely wide, infinitely deep networks. Correlation propagation to infinite depth is possible only at a single critical point in the weight-bias variance plane. At this point, we show that the end-to-end Jacobian vanishes algebraically with depth, and use this to prove that the NTK becomes exactly proportional to the output correlation at infinite depth. This equivalence between information propagation and learning dynamics had not yet been noticed. We further show that orthogonal initialisation suppresses the leading finite-size corrections present under Gaussian initialisation, clarifying the respective roles of the two initialisation ensembles in this limit. These theoretical predictions are validated quantitatively on finite-width, finite-depth networks. Together, these results demonstrate that orthogonal initialisation at criticality plays a central role in controlling the asymptotic dynamics of deep learning.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes a method to realize high-fidelity controlled-phase gates using interacting, distinguishable quantum walkers. By extending the interaction range beyond nearest neighbors, the authors demonstrate that this approach avoids significant fidelity losses inherent in previous designs for indistinguishable particles. The results establish multi-neighbor interactions as a powerful tool for building robust quantum information processing circuits with continuous-time quantum walks.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete guidelines for engineering quantum gates in continuous-time quantum walk models by showing how controlled interactions can overcome limitations associated with particle indistinguishability or complex physical routing.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is implementing high-fidelity controlled-phase (CP) gates using quantum walks.

**Main result.** The proposed architecture using distinguishable particles with extended interactions achieves gate fidelities competitive with, or superior to, previous methods that suffered from fidelity losses due to complex routing gates.

**Method.** The authors derive analytical approximations for gate fidelity by analyzing the scattering process of finite Gaussian wavepackets through interacting quantum walkers.

**Model / system.** The system uses a dual-rail encoding where qubits are realized by quantum walkers on coupled chains. The Hamiltonian includes single-particle tight-binding terms and an extended, distance-dependent interaction term ($H_{int}$).

**Key observables.** Gate fidelity (F), transmission coefficient magnitude and phase derivatives, and the total scattering amplitude $S_{tot}(k_1, k_2)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interaction range extension (multi-neighbor interactions), Gaussian wavepacket width ($\sigma$), and coupling strengths ($J$, $w$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis moves from idealized plane-wave scattering to finite-size Gaussian wavepackets, requiring approximations for the final fidelity calculation.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates CP gate implementations using both indistinguishable (roundabout gates) and distinguishable particles on parallel chains. Figure 2 compares ideal CP gate performance across different interaction types.

**Paper structure.** The paper first motivates the problem by comparing indistinguishable vs. distinguishable particle approaches, then develops the Hamiltonian formalism for interacting walkers, calculates scattering amplitudes using both plane-wave and Gaussian approximations, and finally derives the total gate fidelity based on these calculations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the implementation of controlled-phase (CP) gates with quantum walks in a dual-rail encoding through the use of interacting particles. While previous proposals have focused on indistinguishable particles (bosons or fermions) to achieve unitary fidelity for plane-wave scattering, practical implementations require finite-size wavepackets and routing through single-particle gates, both factors that introduce unavoidable fidelity losses. We show that extending the interaction range beyond on-site or first-neighbor terms provides sufficient control over the scattering potential to engineer CP gates with distinguishable particles that match the ideal bosonic/fermionic performance. For finite Gaussian wavepackets, we derive analytical approximations for the gate fidelity in terms of the transmission coefficient's magnitude and phase derivatives. We find that while distinguishable-particle scattering alone exhibits slightly lower fidelity than the indistinguishable case, the overall architecture that we propose avoids the additional single-particle gates required for routing indistinguishable particles. The roundabout gates needed for the latter indeed introduce fidelity losses approximately one order of magnitude larger than the interaction-induced losses, making the distinguishable-particle approach competitive for practical implementations. Our results establish multi-neighbor interactions as a tool for quantum information processing with continuous-time quantum walks and provide quantitative guidelines for optimizing gate fidelities in finite-size systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This work analyzes an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-symmetric bilayer SLAC fermion model to explore its quantum phase diagram. Using QMC simulations, the authors identify a continuous transition into an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-broken metallic state, followed by a distinct first-order transition into a novel superconducting phase. This provides new insights into Dirac criticality and unconventional superconductivity.

**Why it may be interesting.** The study provides concrete numerical evidence for exotic critical points and superconductivity in strongly interacting fermions, which is highly relevant to understanding unconventional superconductors and quantum criticality beyond simple BCS theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates Dirac criticality beyond standard universality classes and explores novel superconducting states within an interacting fermion model.

**Main result.** The system exhibits a continuous phase transition belonging to the Gross-Neveu-$\mathrm{SO}(3)$ class, followed by a strong-coupling first-order quantum phase transition into an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-symmetric superconducting state.

**Method.** Large-scale Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations and Finite-Size Scaling (FSS) analysis were used to extract critical exponents and characterize the nature of the phase transitions.

**Model / system.** The model is an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-symmetric bilayer SLAC fermion system in $d=2$ dimensions, described by a Hamiltonian with tunable inter-layer interactions ($J$).

**Key observables.** Structure factors for $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ symmetry breaking ($m^2_{\mathrm{SO}(3)}$), superconducting pairing order parameters ($m^2_{SC}$), and critical exponents ($
u, \eta_b$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interaction strength $J$, which drives the system through three regimes: Dirac Semimetal (DSM) $	o$ SO(3)-broken DSM $	o$ SC.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The QMC method is used to probe ground-state expectation values, and comparisons are made between QMC results (suggesting first-order transitions) and mean-field HFB calculations (suggesting continuous coexistence).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing the sequence of transitions; specific plots show data collapse for critical exponents and the abrupt onset of superconducting order parameters at strong coupling.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the system's behavior across increasing interaction strength $J$: first, characterizing the continuous transition to an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-broken phase using QMC; second, investigating the nature of the subsequent strong-coupling instability into a superconducting state by comparing various pairing channels.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The realization of Dirac criticality beyond the conventional Gross-Neveu-Yukawa (GNY) paradigm has become a major frontier in condensed matter physics. In this work, we introduce an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-symmetric bilayer SLAC fermion model with tunable inter-layer interactions that exhibits a rich quantum phase diagram. As the interaction strength increases, the system undergoes two distinct phase transitions. The primary transition is a continuous boundary separating a Dirac semimetal (DSM) from an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-broken ordered phase. Crucially, this transition evades the standard GNY universality class because the emergent order only gaps out a subset of the itinerant fermions. Using large-scale quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations, we establish that this transition belongs to the Gross-Neveu-$\mathrm{SO}(3)$ universality class with $N=6$ irreducible Dirac cones and precisely extract the corresponding critical exponents. At stronger couplings, a second transition drives the system into an inter-layer $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-symmetric superconducting (SC) state. We provide strong numerical evidence that this transition is a quantum-fluctuation-driven first-order transition. Our study provides new insights into the exploration of Dirac criticality beyond the standard GNY universality class, and also offers a novel platform to realize superconductivity featuring $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ symmetry.

</details>

**Summary.** This work develops a structural framework for analyzing quantum resources near black hole horizons by modeling the fermionic transformation as two complementary quantum channels: exterior and interior. The key finding is that these two channels exhibit opposite ordering behaviors with respect to a system parameter $q$. This reveals a universal channel-ordering structure responsible for predictable monotonicity in various quantum correlations.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a structural theory for resource flow in curved spacetime, suggesting that the observed monotonic behavior is dictated by the underlying mathematical structure of the horizon channels rather than the specific physical measure used.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To establish whether monotonic trends observed in relativistic quantum information near black holes stem from specific measurement choices or a universal underlying structural principle.

**Main result.** The exterior and interior fermionic horizon channels exhibit opposite post-processing orders with respect to the channel parameter $q$, leading to predictable monotonicity for various state functionals.

**Method.** Formulating the transformation as complementary quantum channels and analyzing their ordering properties using degradation preorders ($\succeq_{	ext{deg}}$) in both single-mode and multipartite settings.

**Model / system.** The analysis is set in relativistic quantum information theory, specifically modeling fermionic modes near black hole horizons (e.g., GHS dilaton spacetime). The core mathematical tool is the effective single-mode fermionic horizon transformation parameterized by $q$.

**Key observables.** Entanglement, occupation-basis coherence monotones, optimized Bell-functional quantities, and collective coherence based on Quantum Jensen-Shannon divergence (QJSD).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The relativistic channel parameter $q$, which governs the relative weighting between accessible (exterior) and inaccessible (interior) quantum sectors.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework assumes that the relevant mode transformation can be effectively described by a two-level system, allowing for the definition of complementary exterior and interior channels.

**Figures summary.** Not specified in the notes, but numerical evaluation is performed on collective coherence in the GHS black hole spacetime to illustrate predicted homogeneous monotonicity.

**Paper structure.** The paper first introduces the problem by noting ambiguity in resource trends. It then derives the complementary exterior and interior channels ($	ext{E}_{	ext{out}}^q$ and $	ext{E}_{	ext{in}}^q$) and establishes their opposite ordering properties as $q$ changes. Finally, it generalizes this to multipartite settings and connects channel ordering directly to state functional monotonicity.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Relativistic quantum-information studies in noninertial and black-hole settings often determine resource behavior through explicit calculations for particular input states and state functionals, leaving unclear whether the recurring monotonic trends originate from those choices or from a common underlying structure. In this work, we formulate the effective single-mode fermionic horizon transformation as a pair of complementary exterior and interior quantum channels, corresponding respectively to the physically accessible and inaccessible sectors, and establish exact post-processing orders in opposite directions. As the relativistic channel parameter $q$ increases, the exterior channel becomes progressively degraded, whereas the interior channel is ordered in the reverse direction. These relations extend to arbitrary multipartite settings. Consequently, every state functional that is non-increasing under the corresponding intermediate maps is non-increasing in homogeneous exterior sectors and non-decreasing in homogeneous interior sectors. The framework therefore applies to broad classes of quantum resources and correlations, including entanglement and occupation-basis coherence monotones, optimized Bell-functional quantities, and contractive-divergence correlation measures. We further numerically evaluate collective coherence based on the quantum Jensen-Shannon divergence (QJSD) in the Garfinkle-Horowitz-Strominger (GHS) dilaton-black-hole spacetime, illustrating the predicted homogeneous monotonicity. The recurring trends are therefore traced to a common channel-ordering structure, while the physical setting determines the parameterization of $q$ and the resource-theoretic monotonicity determines which output-state quantities inherit the order.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces the 'Magic Scroll,' a novel protocol for enhancing magic state generation in fault-tolerant quantum computing. It achieves this by combining color and bilayer error-correcting codes within multi-qubit register architectures that exploit intrinsic noise bias. The results demonstrate significant, quantifiable improvements (up to 3x) in both magic state cultivation and subsequent distillation volumes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides concrete, mathematically derived protocols that directly address resource limitations (magic state availability) in fault-tolerant quantum computation by integrating hardware constraints (connectivity) with noise characteristics (bias).

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work aims to improve magic state cultivation and distillation procedures in fault-tolerant quantum computation by exploiting high qubit connectivity and intrinsic noise bias.

**Main result.** The proposed 'Magic Scroll' procedure, combining color and bilayer codes, improves magic state cultivation volumes by a factor of 3x and enhances distillation performance similarly.

**Method.** The authors develop efficient implementations for various error-correcting codes (e.g., color codes, bilayer codes) using two-qubit registers and leverage noise bias to enhance these procedures.

**Model / system.** The theoretical framework is built upon multi-qubit register architectures, applicable to platforms like silicon phosphorus qubits or neutral atoms. The analysis focuses on implementing surface and color codes under a biased error model where bit-flip and phase-flip errors are unequal.

**Key observables.** Magic |T> state fidelities (achieving $10^{-9}$), improvement factors for cultivation/distillation volumes ($\sim 3	imes$), and logical error rates ($\epsilon$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Physical error rates ($p$) ranging from $0.05\%$ to $0.1\%$; the bias in noise (Z-errors); and code parameters like graph structures ($6.6.6$, $4.8.8$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions involve using multi-qubit registers for high connectivity, assuming a specific biased error model where idling errors are Z-biased, and employing empirical models for very large patch sizes.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the physical qubit layout of register models, the 'Magic Scroll' procedure combining different codes, performance scaling comparisons between methods at varying physical error rates, and approximations for gapped code performance.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the architectural basis (multi-qubit registers), then detailing the implementation of advanced codes using noise bias, introducing the 'Magic Scroll' procedure to combine these elements, and finally performing detailed performance analysis on distillation volumes using complementary gaps for large patches.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Multiple quantum computing platforms across neutral atoms [1], nitrogen vacancy centres [2, 3], gate-defined dots [4-6] and 14|15 phosphorus atom qubits [7, 8] in silicon are experimentally exploring the use of high connectivity qubits, beyond that of nearest-neighbour planar lattices. Theoretical works consider modifications to fault-tolerant codes to leverage this higher qubit connectivity, such as non-local LDPC codes [9], inspiring superconducting [10] and photonic [11] platforms to also seek non-planar connectivity. In addition, separate theoretical works consider biased noise, where bit- and phase-flip errors are not equally likely. In this work, we present efficient methods for implementing 6.6.6 and 4.8.8 colour codes, as well as bilayer and folded surface codes, using two-qubit registers. We also leverage noise bias to avoid hook errors, demonstrating comparable performance to the surface code. By combining colour and bilayer codes, we show how magic state cultivation procedures [12-14] can be improved, in a procedure we refer to as the Magic Scroll. Not only does the Magic Scroll escape to a standard surface code, it also improves cultivation volumes by 3x and supports magic $|T\rangle$ state fidelities as low as $10^{-9}$. We show that this technique can be further leveraged to improve distillation performance, showing a 3x improvement to distillation volumes for error rates of $\sim 10^{-15}$. Through these constructions, we demonstrate techniques to leverage noise bias and high qubit connectivity, showing how register-based architectures can improve error rates and reduce quantum volumes in fault-tolerant quantum computing.

</details>
