**Summary.** This paper rigorously determines the limiting distribution of the two-replica overlap for the critical Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass model. The key finding is that this distribution converges to a measure defined by the reflected Airy$_1$ point process. This work provides deep mathematical insights into disordered systems, connecting them to established results in random matrix theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on spin glasses, the rigorous mathematical techniques involving convergence of point processes ($\mathrm{Airy}_1$) and scaling limits are highly relevant to understanding critical phenomena in complex quantum many-body systems where disorder is present.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study focuses on determining the distribution of the two-replica overlap ($R_{1,2}$) in the critical Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model.

**Main result.** The quenched distribution of the scaled overlap converges to a random probability measure defined by the reflected Airy$_1$ point process for both Ising and spherical SK models at criticality ($eta=1$).

**Method.** The analysis employs advanced techniques including comparison principles (sphere-to-cube) and passing to scaling limits derived from Gaussian representations, connecting the problem to Random Matrix Theory.

**Model / system.** The system is the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass model, analyzed in both its Ising and spherical variants. The Hamiltonian involves interactions defined by a random matrix $\mathbf{W}$, and the study centers on the Gibbs measure at the critical inverse temperature $eta=1$.

**Key observables.** Two-replica overlap ($R_{1,2}$), quenched distribution of $N^{1/3} R_{1,2}$, and the expectation value $\mathbb{E} \langle R_{1,2}^2 angle$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Critical inverse temperature ($eta=1$), scaling factor $N^{-1/3}$, and convergence to the reflected Airy$_1$ point process.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation for the spherical model relies on representing the Gibbs measure as an anisotropic Gaussian conditioned on norm $\sqrt{N}$. The Ising case uses a comparison principle showing asymptotic coincidence with the spherical case.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the overlap distribution, first establishing general scaling laws and then deriving the specific limiting measure (reflected Airy$_1$ process) for both the spherical and Ising SK models by leveraging connections to Gaussian measures and random matrix theory.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the distribution of the two-replica overlap $R_{1,2}$ in the Ising and spherical Sherrington-Kirkpatrick models at the critical inverse temperature $β= 1$. Our main result shows that in both models, $R_{1,2}$ has scale $N^{-1/3}$, and the quenched distribution of $N^{1/3} R_{1,2}$ converges to an explicit random probability measure defined in terms of the reflected $\mathrm{Airy}_1$ point process. As a consequence, we characterize the limiting value of $N^{2/3} \mathbb{E} \langle R_{1,2}^2 \rangle$, answering a question of Talagrand \cite{talagrand2011mean2}.   For the spherical SK model, we obtain the limit by representing the Gibbs measure as an anisotropic Gaussian on $\mathbb{R}^N$ conditioned to have norm $\sqrt{N}$, and then passing to the $\mathrm{Airy}_1$ scaling limit at the GOE spectral edge. For the Ising SK model, the proof is based on a sphere-to-cube comparison principle showing that the quenched distributions of $N^{1/3} R_{1,2}$ under the spherical and Ising Gibbs measures asymptotically coincide.   This paper is a companion to \cite{du2026fluctuations}, where we introduced a related comparison principle to identify the limiting fluctuations of the SK free energy. Most of the arguments in this paper were generated using GPT-5.6 Pro, with the aim of exploring further consequences of the ideas developed in that work.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically investigates the plasmon modes in nodal line semimetals with quadratic and cubic dispersions using the Random Phase Approximation. It derives distinct carrier-density scaling laws ($\omega_p \sim n^{1/2}$ vs. $\omega_p \sim n^{2/3}$) that serve as unique experimental signatures to distinguish between different topological band structures. The findings establish a robust theoretical framework for understanding collective excitations in these advanced materials.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work provides a detailed theoretical framework for collective dynamics in topological semimetals, linking fundamental band structure properties (quadratic vs. cubic dispersion) directly to measurable optical responses like plasmons via density scaling exponents.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates plasmon modes, which are collective excitations, in higher-order dispersive nodal line semimetals (NLSMs), as these systems are poorly understood compared to their linear counterparts.

**Main result.** Distinct carrier-density scaling laws were found: quadratic NLSMs show $\omega_p \sim n^{1/2}$, while cubic NLSMs exhibit regime-dependent scaling ($\omega_p \sim n^{2/3}$ or $n^{3/4}$).

**Method.** The plasmon frequency is determined by solving the condition $\epsilon(\Omega, q) = 0$ using the Random Phase Approximation (RPA), involving the calculation of the one-loop polarizability from the full Lindhard integral.

**Model / system.** The model considers three-dimensional quadratic and cubic NLSMs characterized by specific Hamiltonian forms. The analysis focuses on calculating the polarization function $\Pi(\Omega, q)$ using both intraband (Drude) and interband contributions.

**Key observables.** Plasmon frequency ($\omega_p$), carrier-density scaling exponents ($n^{1/2}$, $n^{2/3}$), and plasmon anisotropy ratio ($\Omega_z^p / \Omega_\perp^p$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Doping regime characterized by the dimensionless offset $	ilde{k}_Q$, and the validity parameter $r_s$ (Wigner-Seitz radius).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations are performed within the Random Phase Approximation (RPA), which is assumed valid for $r_s \ll 1$. The intraband term is found to dominate the low-energy plasmon response.

**Figures summary.** Figures confirm that the anisotropy ratio $\Gamma_{\perp}/\Gamma_z$ rises from 1.0 at zero doping ($	ilde{k}_Q=0$) to a value near 2 for finite doping, consistent with torus topology.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically derives the density ($n$) first, then calculates the polarization function $\Pi(\Omega, \mathbf{q})$ by separating intraband and interband contributions. Finally, it solves the plasmon dispersion equation using these components to derive the scaling laws for quadratic and cubic NLSMs.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Nodal line semimetals (NLSMs) host distinctive topological properties and unconventional collective excitations. While plasmons in linear NLSMs are well studied, those of higher-order dispersive NLSMs remain poorly understood. We investigate plasmon modes in 3D quadratic and cubic NLSMs within the random phase approximation (RPA), valid for $r_s\ll1$ but breaking down in the small-doping cubic regime where the density of states diverges. Deriving the one-loop polarizability and evaluating its coefficients numerically from the full 3D Lindhard integral, we find distinct carrier-density scaling laws: quadratic NLSMs exhibit $ω_p\sim n^{1/2}$, while cubic NLSMs show $ω_p\sim n^{2/3}$ at large doping crossing over to $ω_p\sim n^{3/4}$ at small doping. The $n^{3/4}$ law is not quantitatively reliable: the diverging density of states drives $r_s>1$ already at $n\sim10^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$, limiting the observable window to at most $10^{18}\lesssim n\lesssim10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$; below this, beyond-RPA correlations are essential. These scalings originate from the power-law density of states and intraband (Drude) response, and are analogous in phase-space power counting to bilayer and trilayer graphene, respectively. The long-wavelength intraband polarization dominates the plasmon frequency, while interband contributions are subleading (two to three orders of magnitude smaller for $Ω\llμ$). Both systems share a plasmon anisotropy $Ω_p^z/Ω_p^\perp\to\sqrt{2}$ in the thin-ring limit, a generic consequence of the torus Fermi-surface geometry. This $\sqrt{2}$ doublet, though observable by HREELS, cannot distinguish quadratic from cubic dispersion; the density scaling exponent is the true distinguishing signature. Our results provide a framework for the collective dynamics of higher-order dispersive NLSMs and suggest experimentally testable signatures accessible by HREELS.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously analyzes classical models of Bell nonlocality when shared randomness is restricted or absent. It shows that these restrictions cause the set of achievable classical correlations to become nonconvex, necessitating advanced mathematical tools beyond simple linear inequalities for characterization. The work culminates in deriving new entropic Bell inequalities applicable to quantum networks with limited shared resources.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on nonlocality, understanding how resource constraints (like limited randomness) fundamentally change the boundary between classical and quantum correlations is a core theoretical problem relevant to designing robust quantum communication protocols.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work investigates how restricting shared randomness affects the set of classical correlations achievable in Bell nonlocality tests, comparing these limits to standard quantum network predictions.

**Main result.** When shared randomness is absent, the classical correlation set becomes nonconvex, requiring multiple linear or nonlinear inequalities (beyond simple Bell functionals) for accurate characterization. The paper derives an entropic Bell inequality specific to limited shared randomness in bipartite scenarios.

**Method.** The authors use optimization techniques, including KKT conditions and analysis of joint conditional probability distributions, to derive necessary constraints on classical correlation functions.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on bipartite Bell scenarios (2-2-2 case) and generalized quantum networks involving multiple sources ($m$ sources, $n$ parties). The core model involves characterizing correlations via local hidden variable models under resource restrictions.

**Key observables.** Bell functions (A, B, C, D), correlation measures ($M_{n,k}, I_{n,k}, J_{n,k}$), and the entropy quantifying shared randomness $H(S)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of parties/sources ($m, n$), the degree of shared randomness (e.g., $|\Lambda|=1$ for no shared randomness).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Initially assumes source independence in standard quantum networks; later relaxes this assumption to analyze correlated sources. A key open question is proving a suggested symmetry between boundary functions.

**Figures summary.** Figure 2 illustrates the feasible regions for classical models with limited shared randomness in $(A, E)$ and $(B, E)$ planes. Figure 4 depicts a star network structure used for analyzing bounds.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from characterizing standard LHV models to handling the nonconvexity arising from zero shared randomness. It then extends this analysis to quantum networks by relaxing source independence assumptions, culminating in deriving specific entropic Bell inequalities.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Bell nonlocality reveals correlations that cannot be explained by classical models and plays a central role in quantum information theory. In this work, we investigate classical models of Bell nonlocality under restrictions on shared randomness. For bipartite scenarios with bounded shared randomness, the set of classical correlations becomes nonconvex. We characterize the correlations achievable without shared randomness through the simultaneous evaluation of multiple linear Bell functionals. We then extend our analysis to quantum networks by relaxing the standard assumption of source independence. In this setting, the feasibility constraints derived for the bipartite case can be used to certify source dependence, and we further construct nonlinear inequalities that distinguish classical models with correlated sources from correlations achievable in standard quantum networks. As an application, we show that these nonlinear network inequalities give rise to an entropic Bell inequality for bipartite scenarios with limited shared randomness.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces QSVM-RQNN, a novel, low-qubit hybrid framework for fault classification tailored for NISQ devices. It combines Quantum Support Vector Machine similarity learning with Recurrent Quantum Neural Networks to process time-series data efficiently. The resulting model shows state-of-the-art performance while maintaining favorable resource efficiency compared to existing quantum methods.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on ML applications, the core development involves designing efficient quantum circuits (low-qubit recurrent architecture) to process complex data representations derived from similarity measures, which touches upon resource optimization in quantum computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing scalable quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms for fault classification on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices while overcoming limitations in qubit resource requirements and noise sensitivity.

**Main result.** The proposed QSVM-RQNN framework achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance-efficiency trade-offs for fault detection on imbalanced datasets.

**Method.** The approach integrates centroid-based Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) similarity learning with Recurrent Quantum Neural Networks (RQNNs), preceded by PCA dimensionality reduction and QSMOTE class balancing.

**Model / system.** The system is a low-qubit hybrid quantum architecture utilizing a compact three-qubit recurrent quantum circuit. It processes feature representations derived from the combination of similarity learning and sequential time steps.

**Key observables.** Fault classification performance, F1-score (especially for minority classes), recall, and robustness against various quantum noise models.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Low qubit count (three qubits); number of recurrent timesteps ($T$) and depth ($L$); dimensionality reduction via PCA.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The framework assumes the feasibility of running on NISQ devices despite resource constraints; performance is evaluated against various established quantum/hybrid baselines.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the overall workflow: PCA $ightarrow$ QSMOTE $ightarrow$ Centroid Construction $ightarrow$ Compact Recurrent Quantum Architecture. Tables detail ablation studies varying $T$ and $L$, and statistical comparisons using average ranks.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem constraints of NISQ devices, proposes the QSVM-RQNN framework with two variants (V1, V2), details preprocessing steps (PCA, QSMOTE), presents ablation studies on architectural parameters ($T, L$), and concludes with performance comparisons against multiple state-of-the-art models.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, limited qubit availability and hardware noise constrain the practical deployment of quantum machine learning (QML). Existing quantum neural network (QNN) and quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN) architectures often require increasing quantum resources as the input dimension grows, limiting scalability on near-term devices. We propose QSVM-RQNN, a low-qubit framework integrating centroid-based Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) similarity learning with Recurrent Quantum Neural Networks (RQNNs) for fault classification. The framework reduces the feature space using principal component analysis (PCA), partitions the reduced representation into sequential timesteps, and processes them using a compact three-qubit recurrent quantum architecture with shared parameters. Two complementary variants are developed: QSVM-RQNN-V1 performs class-conditioned joint quantum encoding of input and centroid segments, whereas QSVM-RQNN-V2 performs recurrent learning over timestep-wise quantum similarity representations. Experimental evaluation on multiple fault diagnosis datasets shows competitive and, in several cases, state-of-the-art performance compared with QSVM, QNN, QCNN, QSVM-QNN, QSVM-QCNN, and RQNN models. The proposed architectures provide favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs, improved recall, and enhanced fault detection on highly imbalanced datasets. These results demonstrate that integrating centroid-based quantum similarity learning with low-qubit recurrent representation learning provides an effective and scalable approach to condition monitoring and fault classification on resource-constrained NISQ devices.

</details>

**Summary.** This work formalizes 'quantum information flow' by translating the concept into the precise mathematical language of string diagrams using the ZX calculus. It distinguishes between superficial path dependencies and genuine, structure-preserving information transfer paths. By showing that complex quantum protocols can be systematically reduced to simple bare wires via rewriting rules, it offers a powerful diagnostic tool for analyzing quantum circuit integrity.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a rigorous, graphical language (ZX calculus) for analyzing how entanglement and quantum information are physically channeled through complex multi-partite protocols, which is foundational knowledge for understanding quantum computation architectures.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to provide an explicit, formal string-diagrammatic definition for the concept of 'quantum information flow,' originally introduced by Coecke.

**Main result.** It formally defines a 'Coecke flow line' based on the compatible inheritance relation within rewriting systems, demonstrating that genuine flow can be tracked through successive diagram rewrites until it reaches a bare wire factor.

**Method.** The authors employ string-diagrammatic rewriting techniques, specifically utilizing the ZX calculus, to model quantum protocols and track information propagation.

**Model / system.** The formalism is illustrated using quantum protocols like teleportation (including GHZ-assisted versions), which are modeled within the framework of dagger compact closed categories.

**Key observables.** The existence and structure of a 'bare wire factor' that represents the information flow after reduction, and the successful simplification of complex diagrams to this bare wire.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Not specified (focus is on structural properties rather than continuous parameters).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the assumption that quantum protocols can be mapped onto string-diagrammatic structures within a dagger compact closed category, and that flow must be certifiable across all measurement branches.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the progression from intuitive flow visualization to ESN construction, formalization as string diagrams (including ZX representations), and finally, step-by-step reduction of complex initial diagrams down to simple bare wires for specific protocol instances.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by revisiting the abstract notion of quantum information flow, developing the mathematical machinery using ESNs and string diagrams in the ZX calculus, and then applying this formalism to concrete examples like teleportation to demonstrate the reduction to a bare wire factor.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We revisit the notion of ``quantum information flow'' introduced in Bob Coecke's early work and seek to give it an explicit string-diagrammatic formalization. Given a semantics preserving string-diagram rewriting sequence, we first distinguish apparent through-paths, which depend on the current graphical presentation, from genuine through paths, which can be compatibly inherited through successive rewrites to a terminal decoupled bare wire factor. We then formally define a ``Coecke flow line'' in terms of this compatible inheritance relation.   In particular, we use the ZX calculus, i.e., the ZX string diagram rewriting system, to illustrate the resulting formalism. In the physical setting of quantum protocols, a Coecke flow can be interpreted as a constrained, quasi-local, line-like presentation of a target bare wire morphism factor within the protocol string diagram.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a unified framework for ensuring the safe disposal (uncomputation) of ancilla qubits in quantum circuits, handling both perfectly initialized ('clean') and arbitrarily initialized ('dirty') states. By proving the problem's computational hardness and introducing the $	ext{RwUn}$ algorithm, it offers state-of-the-art tools that significantly improve circuit synthesis coverage for complex quantum computations.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous theoretical guarantees and practical algorithmic improvements for managing resource qubits in quantum computation, which is foundational knowledge for building reliable quantum compilers and hardware control layers.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the need for automatic, safe uncomputation protocols for auxiliary (ancilla) qubits in quantum circuits, extending coverage from clean to dirty ancillas.

**Main result.** They prove that checking the existence of such an uncomputation is coNP-hard and introduce a rewrite-based normalization algorithm ($	ext{RwUn}$) that achieves high coverage on complex benchmarks compared to existing methods.

**Method.** The authors develop a unified formalization, employing synthesis-oriented techniques like $	ext{RwUn}$ (a rewrite-based normalization) and a template-based reasoning system to structure circuits for safe uncomputation.

**Model / system.** The model is general quantum circuits utilizing ancilla qubits. The focus distinguishes between 'clean' ancillas (known initial state $|0\rangle$) and more complex 'dirty' ancillas (arbitrary, unknown initial state $|x\rangle$).

**Key observables.** Circuit size (S), circuit depth (D), and the ability to restore the ancilla to its original input state $|x\rangle$ for dirty qubits.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The complexity is analyzed based on dependency structures, quantified by 'Aw-Dep' metrics, and performance is benchmarked across various arithmetic circuits (e.g., Adder, Comparator) at increasing scales ($n$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Applicability is limited by the presence of 'aw-cycles' in Boolean circuits or $H$ gates on ancillas/dependent working qubits in general quantum circuits.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate dependency complexity calculations and circuit graphs, while Tables summarize resource requirements (Size/Depth) for various arithmetic families under different uncomputation models ($	ext{Aw-Dep}$, $	ext{RwUn}$, $	ext{Reqomp}$).

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the formal problem definition for clean vs. dirty ancillas, proves the coNP-hardness of existence checking, introduces and details the $	ext{RwUn}$ normalization method, and validates its performance through extensive benchmarking against state-of-the-art tools.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Automatic uncomputation aims to provide programming-language-level support to facilitate the correct and safe use of ancilla qubits in quantum computing, but efforts have only been made for clean ancillas, leaving dirty ancillas unexplored. We present a unified formalization of the uncomputation of both clean and dirty ancillas. For the first time, we prove that checking the existence of uncomputation is coNP-hard. We introduce two complementary synthesis-oriented existence-checking methods: a rewrite-based normalization algorithm (RwUn) and a template-based reasoning system (TpUn) that guarantees uncomputation through structured Store-Use patterns. We implement prototypes of both methods in Qiskit and Python. Compared to the state-of-the-art Reqomp~\cite{reqomp}, RwUn achieves 100% coverage on practical complex-dependency benchmarks, twice the coverage on random classical circuits, and about 50% coverage on random quantum circuits beyond the scope of existing methods, demonstrating broader applicability.

</details>

**Summary.** The paper introduces novel randomized product formulas to simulate quantum dynamics governed by $H = A + \alpha B$. By averaging over random shifts, these methods achieve significantly better error scaling (e.g., $O(\alpha^3)$) than deterministic protocols. This breakthrough is vital for efficiently simulating weakly coupled quantum systems on near-term quantum hardware.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the efficiency bottleneck in quantum simulation algorithms by providing provably superior scaling for time evolution approximations when interactions are weak, which is crucial for simulating many physical systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is developing randomized product formulas that overcome fundamental error scaling limitations inherent in deterministic methods for simulating quantum time evolution.

**Main result.** Randomized formulas achieve superior error scaling, reaching $O(\alpha^3)$ or better, while maintaining a low expected gate overhead compared to the $\Omega(\alpha)$ or $\Omega(\alpha^2)$ lower bounds proven for deterministic counterparts.

**Method.** The authors introduce randomized product formulas by averaging over random shifts in the Trotter steps, which allows error terms that persist deterministically to cancel out through expectation values.

**Model / system.** The simulation targets quantum systems governed by a Hamiltonian $H = A + \alpha B$, where $\alpha$ is small. The analysis considers two access models: one allowing separate exponentials of $A$ and $B$, and a stronger model allowing implementation of $e^{-is(A+\alpha B_\ell)}$ for components $B_\ell$.

**Key observables.** Error scaling (measured by the diamond norm, $\|\cdot\|_\diamond$), expected gate count ($	ext{E}_\omega[G]$), and comparison against lower bounds.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The small coupling strength $\alpha$, the number of Trotter steps ($r$), and the order of approximation ($2k$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on $\alpha \ll 1$ and uses techniques like Dyson series expansions, telescoping identities, and bounding mixed derivatives.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate schematics comparing deterministic vs. randomized formulas (Fig. 1), detail the dyadic sampling strategy for THRIFT (Fig. 2), and benchmark gate counts/error scaling for physical models (Figs. 3 & 4).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes two access models, deriving improved error bounds using randomization techniques based on Trotter-Heuristic Resource Improved Formulas (THRIFT) and establishing corresponding lower bounds that prove the necessity of randomization.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Product formulas, also known as Trotter formulas, are among the most widely used and practical methods for simulating quantum systems on quantum computers. Here we introduce two new classes of randomized product formulas for simulating Hamiltonians with separated energy scales, $H=A+αB$, where $α$ is small. In the standard access model, where one can implement exponentials of $A$ and $B$ separately, our randomized formulas achieve $\mathcal O(α^2)$ error scaling at the cost of only doubling the gate depth of the corresponding deterministic formula. We further prove an $Ω(α)$ lower bound for deterministic product formulas. In a stronger access model, allowing exponentials of $A+αB_\ell$ for $B = \sum_{\ell}B_\ell$, our randomized formula, based on Trotter Heuristic Resource Improved Formulas for Time-dynamics (THRIFT)~[J. L. Bosse et al., Nat. Commun. 16, 2673 (2025)], achieves $\mathcal O(α^3)$ error scaling with only constant-factor expected gate overhead. We also establish an $Ω(α^2)$ lower bound for deterministic product formulas in this access model. Numerical simulations confirm gate-count reductions for simulating physically motivated systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the Gibbs Paradox by developing a statistical mechanics framework that incorporates local free space and collision potentials. Instead of relying on quantum indistinguishability arguments, it rederives the entropy increase for gas mixtures using the canonical ensemble. The resulting formula suggests that the entropy change depends on specific molecular properties, thus resolving the paradox in a novel way.

**Why it may be interesting.** It offers a non-standard statistical mechanical approach to a classic problem, linking macroscopic entropy changes directly to microscopic, time-dependent potential energy interactions during mixing.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to resolve the Gibbs Paradox—the discrepancy regarding entropy increase upon gas mixing—without invoking the concept of identical particles.

**Main result.** By incorporating local free space and collision potential energy into the canonical ensemble calculation, the authors derive a non-zero entropy increase formula ($\Delta S$) that depends on specific gas properties.

**Method.** The methodology involves rederiving the entropy change using the canonical ensemble approach, treating molecular interactions via collision potentials rather than relying solely on ideal gas assumptions.

**Model / system.** The model is an ideal gas mixture undergoing mixing. Interactions are governed by local free space volume and a potential energy term derived from collisions between different types of molecules (Gas 1 and Gas 2).

**Key observables.** Entropy increase ($\Delta S$), Free Energy ($F$), Collision Potential Energy ($\epsilon_p$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Molecular mass, effective radius, collision characteristic time, number densities ($n_1, n_2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions are that collisions are the main interaction force and that the local free space volume dictates molecular movement, allowing avoidance of the $N!$ factor.

**Figures summary.** Figures schematically illustrate the time dependence of various collision potential energies ($\epsilon_{1p}, \epsilon_{2p}, \epsilon_{mp}$).

**Paper structure.** The paper reviews existing solutions to the Gibbs paradox, develops a framework based on local free space and collision potentials using the canonical ensemble, derives $\Delta S$ by considering interaction potentials, and concludes with an expression showing property dependence.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

This paper argues that the Gibbs paradox can be resolved without using the concept of identical particles in quantum mechanics. The molecules in different regions of the gas can be distinguished, so there is no need to introduce the N! factor. For each molecule, the volume of its free movement space is local at every instant. Moreover, collisions are the primary way of interaction between gas molecules and the fundamental driving force for reaching equilibrium. The potential energy during collisions cannot be ignored. Based on the local free space assumption and collision potential energy, this paper uses the canonical ensemble method to rederive the entropy increase formula for gas mixtures. It includes parameters such as molecular mass, effective radius, and collision characteristic time, which vary with the type of gas molecules. This solves the problem that the entropy increase of gas mixtures is independent of gas properties, that is, it truly resolves the Gibbs paradox instead of providing a new conceptual explanation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a systematic method using Krylov spread complexity to probe black hole interiors holographically. By analyzing the BTZ black hole dual to a 2D CFT, the authors show that the complexity exhibits quadratic late-time growth ($\gamma=2$), which requires careful resummation of infinite series invariants. This work provides a powerful new tool linking quantum dynamics (Krylov theory) directly to gravitational thermodynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work connects concepts from quantum information (complexity measures), general relativity (black holes/BTZ geometry), and advanced mathematical physics (spectral theory via Krylov methods). The focus on non-trivial asymptotic scaling ($\gamma=2$ vs $\gamma=1$) is highly relevant to understanding the deep structure of holographic entanglement and complexity.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is determining a robust boundary quantity that accurately captures the growth of black-hole interiors quantified by holographic complexity, especially beyond simple 2D gravity models.

**Main result.** The authors establish that for the BTZ black hole dual to CFT2, Krylov spread complexity exhibits an intermediate departure from early-time quadratic growth, followed by behavior compatible with asymptotically quadratic growth ($\gamma=2$).

**Method.** The work employs a combination of holographic duality (relating bulk geometry to boundary quantum dynamics), the moment method applied to Lanczos recursion for Krylov spread complexity, and advanced asymptotic analysis techniques like Padé continuation.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on black holes, specifically the BTZ black hole in 2D, which is dual to a large-central-charge two-dimensional conformal field theory (CFT). A benchmark system used for comparison is the double-scaled Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev (DSSYK) model.

**Key observables.** Krylov spread complexity ($C_K(t)$), generalized complexity built from extrinsic-curvature invariants, and the asymptotic growth rate ($\gamma$) of this complexity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis examines different time/temperature regimes (early vs. late times) and requires careful handling of the order in which semiclassical limits are taken relative to the reconstruction of the complexity measure.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Key assumptions include the validity of holographic duality for these systems and the necessity of resumming infinite series expansions (like those involving extrinsic-curvature invariants) to capture the correct asymptotic behavior.

**Figures summary.** The notes describe a comparison between finite truncations of an expansion (showing linear growth, $\gamma=1$) and the fully resummed function (showing quadratic growth, $\gamma=2$), illustrating the non-commutativity of limits.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first identifying the theoretical gap in complexity measures, then using the DSSYK model as a controlled benchmark to establish an 'order-of-limits' rule. It then applies this framework to the BTZ black hole/CFT2 system, deriving and analyzing the resulting asymptotic behavior of $C_K(t)$ through detailed mathematical expansions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The boundary quantity that captures the growth of black-hole interiors quantified by holographic complexity remains unknown beyond 2d dilaton gravity. We provide a critical analysis of a partition-function construction of Krylov spread complexity for thermofield-double states that provides a dimension-independent boundary reconstruction from semiclassical holographic partition functions, while developing the present dynamical and bulk construction for the BTZ saddle. In the double-scaled Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, where exact and semiclassical results can be compared, we show that the classical limit is reliable only when taken after the complexity has been reconstructed; taking this limit at the level of individual Lanczos coefficients discards essential information. Applying the construction to a large-central-charge two-dimensional conformal field theory above the Hawking-Page temperature dual to a Bañados-Teitelboim-Zanelli black hole, we find an intermediate departure from early-time quadratic growth followed by behavior compatible with a return toward asymptotically quadratic growth, rather than the linear late-time behavior of the volume and the standard finite-functional complexity = anything class. We then match this boundary behavior to a generalized complexity = anything bulk object built from an infinite series of extrinsic-curvature invariants. The construction provides a systematic route from black-hole thermodynamics to Krylov dynamics and can naturally be extended to higher-dimensional holographic black holes.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper tackles the lack of standardization in tracking quantum computation history (provenance) across diverse quantum hardware providers. The authors propose a unified, evidence-aware OpenAPI contract and an adapter architecture to normalize this fragmented data. This framework is vital for achieving reproducibility and interoperability in the rapidly evolving field of quantum computing.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Quantum software development suffers from a 'provenance-integration problem' because different quantum hardware providers expose necessary provenance data through heterogeneous, non-standardized APIs.

**Main result.** The authors propose an evidence-aware OpenAPI 3.1 contract and provider-adapter architecture that successfully normalizes provenance records while preserving provider-specific semantics.

**Method.** The methodology involves a comparative analysis of 15 quantum platforms' public documentation, followed by designing and testing a fixture-backed reference prototype covering major providers (Braket, IBM, IonQ).

**Model / system.** The focus is on the abstract concept of Quantum Provenance—the comprehensive audit trail describing programs, compilation steps, execution conditions, hardware characterization, and results for quantum computations.

**Key observables.** Provenance records (including 21 validated attributes in prototype tests), evidence origins, and structured metadata about computation history.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The scope covers five hardware technologies: superconducting, trapped-ion, neutral-atom, photonic, and quantum-annealing devices.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The evaluation is limited to public interface documentation and sanitized fixtures; it does not cover live field population or production deployment complexities.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 (mentioned in notes) summarizes the four-stage design process: literature review $ightarrow$ comparative analysis $ightarrow$ API artifact development $ightarrow$ industrial demonstration.

**Paper structure.** The paper follows a Design Science Research approach, moving from identifying the need for standardized provenance (RQ1/Literature Review), to analyzing current provider gaps (RQ2/Comparative Analysis), designing the unified OpenAPI contract and adapters (RQ3/Design Principles), and finally demonstrating feasibility with a prototype (RQ4/Evaluation).

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum software development requires provenance describing programs, compilation, execution, hardware characterization, results, and software environments, but providers expose this information through heterogeneous software development kits, application programming interfaces, and resource models. We analyze publicly documented provenance access across 15 quantum platforms spanning five hardware technologies and find fragmented, incomplete coverage, with compilation provenance weakest. We propose an evidence-aware OpenAPI 3.1 provenance contract and provider-adapter architecture, evaluated through a fixture-backed reference prototype at QMill covering Amazon Braket, IBM Quantum, and IonQ. All records validate against one common contract while preserving provider-specific semantics, explicit evidence origins, and graceful handling of incomplete data.

**Summary.** The paper investigates the distillability of negative-partial-transpose quantum states by testing if one-copy-undistillable states become distillable with multiple copies. Using fixed witnesses and tensor product constructions, the authors prove that a specific state family is two-copy distillable for all dimensions $d \geq 3$. This result significantly refines our understanding of entanglement boundaries in quantum information theory.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides rigorous mathematical proofs regarding entanglement properties (distillability) in structured quantum states, which is foundational knowledge for understanding resource theories in quantum information processing.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is determining if negative-partial-transpose (NPT) states, which are undistillable from a single copy, become distillable when multiple copies are available.

**Main result.** The authors prove that a specific one-copy-undistillable state within the canonical family is two-copy distillable in every dimension $d \geq 3$, contradicting previous conjectures about its persistence of undistillability.

**Method.** The study employs constructing fixed quantum witnesses (e.g., $|\Psi_dangle$) whose expectation values are calculated on tensor products of the state to test for negative entanglement measures indicative of distillability.

**Model / system.** The analysis focuses on bipartite quantum states $ho$ exhibiting NPT, specifically utilizing a canonical two-parameter family introduced by DiVincenzo et al. The results hold for arbitrary local dimensions $d \geq 3$.

**Key observables.** Distillability status (one-copy vs. two-copy), and the sign of expectation values calculated using fixed witnesses.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The local dimension $d$, and the state parameters $(b, c)$ defining the canonical family $ho_{b,c}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derived bounds are based on analytic fixed witnesses and do not necessarily represent the fully optimized distillability boundaries.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the parameter plane for NPT states in $d=3$, showing regions certified as two-copy distillable (blue lobe) versus those whose status is unresolved, comparing results from two-copy vs. three-copy witnesses.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically investigates the distillability of canonical NPT states by first establishing a two-copy witness for general $d \geq 3$, then constructing and analyzing stronger three-copy witnesses, and finally mapping out the resulting certified regions on the parameter plane.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Whether negative-partial-transpose (NPT) states that are undistillable from one copy become distillable from finitely many copies remains a basic open problem in entanglement theory. We study the canonical two-parameter family of DiVincenzo \textit{et al.}, introduced as a symmetry-reduced testbed for this question. We prove that a distinguished one-copy-undistillable state in this family is already two-copy distillable in every local dimension $d\geq 3$. A uniform equal-norm tight-frame construction gives explicit Schmidt-rank-two certificates in every dimension, thereby disproving the conjecture that the entire one-copy-undistillable region of the canonical family remains undistillable for arbitrarily many copies. The same witnesses certify an open two-copy-distillable neighborhood around the counterexample, while separately constructed three-copy witnesses enlarge the inner bounds for the distillable region in the surrounding parameter space. In contrast, recent results for Werner states, together with the propagation argument of DiVincenzo \textit{et al.}, establish a neighboring region of one-copy-undistillable states that remains two-copy undistillable. Thus a single symmetry-reduced family contains rigorously certified states with opposite two-copy behavior, separated by a substantial region whose finite-copy distillability remains unresolved.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Many industrial optimization tasks can be modeled as graph coloring, where adjacent vertices must have different colors. This NP-hard problem is challenging for large graphs. We present a quantum encoding requiring qubits that scale logarithmically with the number of colors and linearly with vertices. Using adiabatic evolution with a novel mixer Hamiltonian and vertex terms, we compute the chromatic number and demonstrate robustness by solving constrained truck loading problems.

**Summary.** This theoretical paper determines an upper bound for the purity ($	ext{Tr}(ho^2)$) of bipartite quantum states satisfying the Absolutely Positive Partial Transpose (APPT) condition. By reformulating the problem as a constrained optimization over the eigenvalues, the authors derive explicit bounds dependent on the dimensions of the subsystems. This work contributes to understanding the fundamental limitations on state purity for highly structured quantum correlations.

**Why it may be interesting.** Understanding purity bounds for specific classes of quantum states like APPT is crucial for characterizing entanglement and resource theories in quantum information, directly impacting protocols relying on state distinguishability.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to derive an upper bound for the purity ($	ext{Tr}(ho^2)$) of quantum states that are Absolutely Positive Partial Transpose (APPT). This bound also applies to absolutely separable bipartite states.

**Main result.** The paper establishes a general, piecewise-defined upper bound for the maximum purity based on $k = mn \pmod{4}$, providing explicit formulas derived from analyzing the vertices of an associated convex polytope.

**Method.** The analysis involves formulating the problem as maximizing a quadratic function of eigenvalues ($\sum \lambda_i^2$) subject to linear constraints defining a polytope, which is solved by checking the extreme points (vertices) of this set.

**Model / system.** The study concerns bipartite quantum states $ho$ acting on $H_A \otimes H_B$, where $m = \dim H_A$ and $n = \dim H_B$. The concepts revolve around separability criteria like PPT and APPT.

**Key observables.** Purity ($	ext{Tr}(ho^2)$), which quantifies how close the state is to a pure state, and the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of the density matrix $ho$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimensions $m$ and $n$, and their product $k=mn$, particularly its value modulo 4.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the maximum purity is attained at a vertex of the defined polytope, allowing for optimization over these extreme points.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the definitions of separable and APPT states, then formulates the problem as an optimization task on the eigenvalue space. It proceeds by analyzing the constraints defining a convex polytope $S_k$ and deriving explicit bounds (Theorem 1) based on the congruence class of $mn$.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

A quantum state is called absolutely separable (resp. absolutely positive partial transpose (APPT)) if it remains separable (resp. positive partial transpose (PPT)) under any global unitary transformation. It is known that the set of all absolutely separable states is a subset of the set of all APPT states. Moreover, these two sets are identical for qubit-qudit systems. In this note, we give an upper bound for the purity of APPT bipartite states (and therefore for the purity of absolutely separable bipartite states). For qubit-qudit systems, this upper bound becomes the maximum purity of APPT (and absolutely separable) states.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a Quantum DevOps workflow designed to monitor 'transpilation drift,' which occurs when compiler updates change the compiled form of a quantum circuit even if the source code remains identical. By calculating structural metrics and integrating checks into CI/CD pipelines, it provides an essential, auditable guardrail for ensuring reproducibility in quantum software development.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on software engineering rather than physical dynamics, understanding how compilation choices affect circuit structure is crucial for designing robust quantum algorithms that are portable across evolving hardware platforms.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is detecting 'transpilation drift,' where changes in evolving quantum compiler toolchains cause an unchanged source circuit to compile into a structurally different target realization.

**Main result.** The authors propose and demonstrate a practical Quantum DevOps workflow that uses structural metrics to detect these compilation-induced changes before hardware execution, making the process observable and auditable.

**Method.** They implement a CI/CD guardrail that transpiles circuits against target profiles, calculates a structural drift metric (D_struct) comparing current artifacts to stored baselines, and reports status via configurable thresholds in GitHub Actions.

**Model / system.** The focus is on the compilation process itself, using abstract quantum circuits (like QFT10 or BV12) as inputs that are mapped onto specific hardware backends defined by target profiles and SDK versions.

**Key observables.** Structural metrics including circuit depth, total gate count, two-qubit gate counts, and the calculated structural drift score (D_struct).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Configurable warning ($	au_{	ext{warn}}$) and failure ($	au_{	ext{fail}}$) thresholds used to classify the CI status.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary limitation is that the measured drift is a structural proxy; it does not guarantee semantic non-equivalence or predict actual execution fidelity, and threshold calibration is left for future work.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the full workflow pipeline (transpile -> measure -> compare to baseline -> pass/warn/fail) integrated with MLflow logging. Table II provides a detailed comparison of metrics across different transpiler versions.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem, details the proposed Quantum DevOps workflow and structural drift metric calculation, demonstrates its utility using scenarios like seed drift and toolchain upgrades (e.g., Qiskit 2.1.2 vs 2.4.2), and concludes by establishing the CI guardrail.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum software workflows rely on compiler and provider toolchains that evolve independently of application source code. Consequently, an unchanged quantum circuit may transpile into a different target-specific realization after changes in SDK versions, optimization settings, basis gates, coupling maps, or backend descriptions. Such transpilation drift can affect circuit depth, gate composition, qubit mapping, and execution behavior, yet it is rarely monitored in CI/CD pipelines. This paper proposes a Quantum DevOps workflow for detecting transpilation drift before execution. The workflow transpiles source circuits against configured target profiles, computes structural drift metrics, records provenance and artifacts in MLflow, and raises configurable warnings or failures in GitHub Actions. Using representative circuits and target profiles, we show how drift checks can expose toolchain-induced changes and support reproducibility audits. The contribution is a practical CI/CD guardrail for making quantum compilation behavior observable, testable, and auditable.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper mathematically proves that 2D translation-invariant topological CSS codes can always be locally unitarily decoupled into a combination of toric codes and product states. The authors provide an efficient algorithm based on module theory over Laurent polynomials to construct this decoupling map, simplifying the understanding and implementation of these quantum error-correcting codes.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous mathematical tools (module theory) to simplify complex quantum error-correcting codes into known, simpler structures (toric codes), which is fundamental for building scalable quantum computation architectures.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To prove that no further obstruction exists beyond removing anyon-permuting translations when decoupling 2D translation-invariant topological CSS codes into toric codes and product states.

**Main result.** The authors prove this non-existence of obstruction, showing every such code admits a local unitary decoupling into toric codes and product states after passing to the maximal anyon-preserving superlattice.

**Method.** The core method involves applying module theory over Laurent polynomials ($R = \mathbb{F}_2[x\pm 1, y\pm 1]$) and advanced linear algebra techniques to find required chain isomorphisms between complex structures.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on two-dimensional (2D) translation-invariant topological Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes defined by Pauli Hamiltonians. These are analyzed using module theory over the Laurent polynomial ring, relating them to toric codes and product states.

**Key observables.** Logical error rate, support spreading $s(Q)$, number of e-anyons ($t$), and the existence/invertibility of chain isomorphisms.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The density of qubits per unit cell ($q$) and the dimensions related to stabilizer generators ($r$ and $s$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Previous constructions break more symmetry than necessary; the analysis relies on module theory over non-field rings, which complicates standard linear algebra techniques.

**Figures summary.** One figure summary mentions a speed-accuracy tradeoff comparison between decoding methods (unitary-decouple vs. BP-OSD), and another table quantifies support spreading for transported CNOTs.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the mathematical framework using module theory over Laurent polynomials, proves the existence of the decoupling map via chain isomorphism construction, provides an efficient algorithm to compute this map, and discusses applications like gate construction and decoding performance.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Two-dimensional translation-invariant topological CSS codes on qubits are known to be locally equivalent, after coarse-graining, to stacks of toric codes. However, existing constructions generally break more translation symmetry than is required to remove anyon-permuting translations, leaving open whether any further obstruction exists. We prove that no such obstruction occurs: after passing to the maximal anyon-preserving superlattice, every such code admits a local unitary decoupling into toric codes and product states. We further provide an efficient algorithm for explicitly constructing the decoupling map, together with bounds on the required supercell size and operator spreading. The decoupling requires no additional ancillas in generic cases and extends to finite systems with suitable boundary conditions.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper calculates the covering radius associated with the single-qubit Clifford gate set embedded in SU(2). By mapping the problem onto a minimization task on SO(3), the authors precisely determine this radius to be arccos(sqrt(5)/6). This result quantifies a fundamental geometric limit on the fidelity achievable by sequences of Clifford gates.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides deep mathematical insights into the fundamental structure of quantum gate sets, which is crucial for understanding universal quantum computation and resource estimation in quantum information theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper determines the covering radius of the topological closure of the single-qubit Clifford hierarchy within SU(2) (identified with S^3). This is equivalent to finding the minimum all-level Clifford fidelity.

**Main result.** The covering radius is found to be arccos(sqrt(5)/6), and the extremal points, called 'deep holes', form a single orbit of size 192 under Clifford gate multiplication.

**Method.** The problem is solved by mapping the geometry from S^3 to SO(3) via a quaternionic double cover. This reduces the covering problem to an exact minimax statement concerning the L-infinity norm on SO(3).

**Model / system.** The system models the single-qubit quantum gate space, represented by SU(2) or S^3. The structure analyzed is the closure of the Clifford hierarchy, which forms a union of 18 great circles in this space.

**Key observables.** The covering radius $ho(U_{18})$ and the minimum all-level Clifford fidelity (which equals $5/6$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The size of the deep hole orbit (192) and the value $\sqrt{5}/6$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof relies on identifying the configuration of planes as a Grassmannian 3-design and utilizing the specific structure provided by the quaternionic double cover to map the problem onto SO(3).

**Paper structure.** The paper first defines the geometry (18 circles in S^3) and establishes an orthonormal basis for their projectors. It then maps the covering problem from S^3 to a minimax statement on SO(3), solving this final geometric minimization problem.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We determine the covering radius of the topological closure of the single-qubit Clifford hierarchy in $\SU(2)\cong S^3$. This closure is a union of $18$ great circles --- the Clifford--Pauli circles --- and we prove that its covering radius is $\arccos\sqrt{5/6}$. The extremal points, which we call \emph{deep holes}, form a single orbit of size $192$ under left and right multiplication by Clifford gates, and are described in closed form. Equivalently, the minimum over one-qubit unitaries of the all-level Clifford fidelity is $5/6$. The proof rests on two structures attached to the configuration of $18$ planes in $\R^4$: their centered rank-two projectors form an orthonormal basis of the irreducible $\SO(4)$-module $\Sym_0(4)$, and the projection profile of a unit quaternion is exactly its image under the double cover $\SU(2)\to\SO(3)$. These reduce the covering problem to a minimax statement for the $\ell^\infty$-norm on $\SO(3)$ which we solve exactly, classifying its equality cases.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops the theory and constructions for entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes (EAQLRCs) with availability. It establishes fundamental bounds and provides explicit examples derived from algebraic geometry codes, showing how shared entanglement allows for multiple independent recovery sets. This advances the field of fault-tolerant quantum memory by offering robust coding schemes for erasure correction.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly contributes to the theoretical framework of quantum data storage and fault tolerance, providing concrete construction methods that improve upon standard Quantum CSS code limitations by incorporating shared entanglement for enhanced local repair capabilities.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The work focuses on defining, bounding, and constructing entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes (EAQLRCs) that allow for fault tolerance against erasures.

**Main result.** They establish a Singleton-like bound for EAQLRCs and provide explicit constructions using various classical code families, including those derived from algebraic geometry curves.

**Method.** The authors use techniques from classical coding theory (e.g., linear codes, folding) combined with quantum information concepts to construct the codes and derive their parameters.

**Model / system.** The model is abstract quantum error correction applied to data storage, specifically addressing erasure channels where the location of lost qubits is known. The underlying mathematical structures are based on classical linear codes and algebraic geometry curves over finite fields.

**Key observables.** Code parameters such as length ($n$), quantum dimension ($k_Q$), locality ($r$), availability ($t$), and minimum distance ($d_{EA}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The key parameters are the erasure tolerance ($\delta-1$) and the number of local recovery sets available ($t$). The construction relies on shared entanglement.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The definition assumes an erasure model where the positions of lost qubits are known. A major assumption is that the receiver's halves of the ebits are not subject to noise.

**Figures summary.** The notes mention comparative tables (Table 1 and Table 2) summarizing dimension bounds and parameters for different types of quantum local recovery codes derived from various classical families.

**Paper structure.** The paper proceeds by reviewing necessary background in coding theory, formally defining EAQLRCs with availability, presenting random constructions using Vandermonde matrices, detailing explicit constructions from algebraic-geometry codes (like Hermitian and Suzuki), and concluding with open problems.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

In this work, we define entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes with availability, in which any set of up to $δ-1$ erased qudits can be recovered from any one of $t$ local recovery sets, each of size at most $r+δ-1$, with the recovery sets intersecting exactly in the erased coordinates, where $r$ is a (small) positive integer. We show that shared entanglement permits $t>1$, meaning that multiple local recovery sets can be available for the same set of up to $δ-1$ erasures. We establish a Singleton-like bound for this family of codes and present random constructions based on classical linear codes with Vandermonde parity-check matrices. We also provide explicit constructions of entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes with availability from several classical code families and their folded versions, including Tamo-Barg codes, fiber-product codes, and algebraic-geometry codes such as one-point Hermitian and Suzuki codes.

</details>

**Why it may be interesting.** While not directly about physical Hamiltonians, the development of quantum algorithms for solving complex optimization problems like MOT is highly relevant. Quantum speedups in linear programming solvers are a major area of theoretical interest that could impact simulations in physics (e.g., calculating free energy differences or correlation functions via optimal transport metrics).

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is developing efficient algorithms, both classical and quantum, to approximate the multimarginal optimal transport (MOT) distance between multiple discrete probability distributions.

**Main result.** The authors present a classical algorithm with a specific polynomial runtime bound and two distinct quantum algorithms—a projected subgradient method and a Sinkhorn variant—that achieve dimension speedups over classical counterparts.

**Method.** The work uses techniques from convex optimization, formulating MOT as a linear program (LP) or its dual. Quantum approaches leverage quantum subroutines to accelerate the iterative solving of these LPs.

**Model / system.** The model is purely mathematical/algorithmic: approximating the distance between $m$ discrete probability distributions ($\mu_1, \dots, \mu_m$), each supported on at most $n$ points. The problem structure generalizes classical Optimal Transport (OT).

**Key observables.** The primary observable is the MOT distance itself, approximated within an additive error $\varepsilon$. Other key quantities include the coupling tensor $X$ and its expected transportation cost.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Key parameters are $m$ (number of marginals), $n$ (support size), and $\varepsilon$ (desired accuracy). The complexity analysis depends heavily on these values.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The quantum algorithms estimate the cost rather than returning an explicit coupling tensor, except in the case of the Sinkhorn algorithm which returns an implicit description. The classical bounds are derived for general MOT problems.

**Figures summary.** No specific figure summaries were extracted; the notes focus on algorithmic complexity and theoretical results presented across different methods (Primal/Dual LPs).

**Paper structure.** The paper is structured around formulating the MOT problem as an LP, presenting classical solutions for the primal form, and then detailing two distinct quantum algorithms—one based on projected subgradients applied to the dual, and another using a quantum Sinkhorn method for entropy regularization.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study algorithms for approximating the multimarginal optimal transport (MOT) distance, a generalization of the classic optimal transport distance, between $m$ discrete probability distributions each supported on at most $n$ points. We give a classical algorithm that computes a coupling between these marginals whose expected transportation cost is within an additive $\varepsilon > 0$ of the MOT distance in time $O(m^2 n^m \varepsilon^{-1}\mathrm{polylog}(m,n,\varepsilon^{-1}))$. This is, to our knowledge, the first bound for general MOT problems with simultaneous linear dependence on the dimension $n^m$ and on the accuracy parameter $\varepsilon^{-1}$, improving the prior state of the art.   On the quantum side, we give two algorithms that achieve speedups in dimension, though with worse accuracy dependence than classical approaches. First, we construct a quantum projected subgradient method for estimating the MOT distance within an additive $\varepsilon >0$ with runtime $O( m^3 n^{\frac{m}{2}+1} \varepsilon^{-2} \mathrm{polylog}(m,n,\varepsilon^{-1}))$. This algorithm works with the linear programming dual of the MOT problem, and does not return a coupling. We also give a quantum multimarginal Sinkhorn algorithm for entropy-regularized MOT. This algorithm returns an implicit description of an approximately optimal coupling with runtime $O(m^8n^{\frac{m+1}{2}} \varepsilon^{-5} \mathrm{polylog}(m,n,\varepsilon^{-1})))$ after the usual reduction from entropic MOT to unregularized MOT. We also record query lower bounds: for any precision $\varepsilon<1/2$, randomized classical algorithms require $Ω(n^m/(1+\varepsilon n))$ queries and quantum algorithms require $Ω(\sqrt{n^m/(1+\varepsilon n)})$ queries.

</details>

**Summary.** This work uses first-principles calculations to map the microscopic origin of spin splitting in altermagnetic CrSb thin films. The authors find that surface termination is crucial, showing that robust spin splitting requires specific long-range inter-unit-cell hopping pathways unique to certain surfaces. This establishes a general principle for controlling electronic properties by engineering low-dimensional crystal interfaces.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on magnetism, understanding how crystal symmetry and dimensionality fundamentally alter electronic band structure via orbital hybridization (hopping) provides a generalizable principle for engineering quantum properties in novel materials systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study aims to resolve the microscopic origin of spin splitting in altermagnetic CrSb thin films, specifically investigating how this property changes when dimensionality is reduced from bulk to 2D.

**Main result.** The paper demonstrates that surface orientation dictates the electronic structure; while the (2$ar{1}ar{1}0$) slab retains strong spin splitting, others do not. This splitting fundamentally relies on long-range inter-unit-cell coplanar Cr--Sb hopping pathways.

**Method.** First-principles calculations were used to model CrSb slabs with various surface orientations and varying vacuum spacings to simulate dimensional reduction. Wannier tight-binding Hamiltonians were constructed to analyze the contribution of different hopping channels.

**Model / system.** The physical system is metallic CrSb, an altermagnet known for its giant spin splitting. The model involves constructing slab geometries with specific surface terminations ((2$ar{1}ar{1}0$), (0001), etc.) and systematically varying the inter-slab vacuum spacing to tune coupling strength.

**Key observables.** Momentum-dependent spin splitting magnitude, electronic band structures along high-symmetry k-paths, and the contribution of specific hopping parameters ($	ext{Cr–Sb}$, $	ext{Sb–Sb}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Dimensionality (3D bulk vs. 2D thin film limit), surface orientation, and inter-unit-cell coupling strength.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The calculations assume that the electronic structure can be accurately modeled by analyzing the contributions of specific hopping pathways derived from first-principles results.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the crystal structures for different planes, show the evolution of spin splitting as vacuum spacing changes (comparing surfaces), and detail how retaining specific inter-unit-cell hopping terms is necessary to reproduce the observed spin splitting in the most stable surface orientation.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares the electronic structure of bulk vs. various slab geometries using first-principles calculations, then refines this analysis by constructing Wannier Hamiltonians and analyzing the necessity of specific long-range hopping terms ($	ext{Cr–Sb}$ vs $	ext{Sb–Sb}$) to explain the observed spin splitting in low dimensions.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Altermagnets have recently emerged as promising materials for spintronic applications owing to their momentum-dependent spin splitting. Among them, metallic CrSb is particularly attractive owing to its giant spin splitting and high Néel temperature. However, the microscopic origin of the distinct spin-splitting behaviors in bulk and thin-film CrSb remains unresolved. Here, we systematically investigate the electronic structures of CrSb slabs with different surface orientations using first-principles calculations. Although all considered slabs preserve spin-group symmetries compatible with altermagnetism, they exhibit markedly different electronic structures: the (2$\bar{1}\bar{1}$0) slab retains pronounced altermagnetic spin splitting, whereas the (0001) and (10$\bar{1}$0) slabs display nearly spin-degenerate bands. We demonstrate that dimensional reduction fundamentally changes the microscopic origin of altermagnetic spin splitting. Unlike bulk CrSb, altermagnetic spin splitting in thin films requires long-range inter-unit-cell coplanar Cr--Sb hopping, while Sb--Sb hopping provides an additional contribution. The preservation or suppression of these hopping pathways explains the strong surface dependence of the spin splitting. Our findings establish a microscopic mechanism for understanding altermagnetism in reduced dimensions and provide a general principle for engineering spin splitting in low-dimensional altermagnetic materials.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework designed to overcome the difficult search problem associated with finding practical Quantum LDPC codes. By combining specialist proposal, memory retention, and iterative program execution, the agents efficiently discover high-performing code candidates. These results provide concrete, hardware-relevant quantum error correction resources for future experimental implementation.

**Why it may be interesting.** The application of advanced AI techniques to systematically discover optimal quantum error correction codes is highly relevant. It provides a blueprint for using computational intelligence to solve fundamental theoretical limits in quantum computation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is designing practical, finite-length Quantum Low-Density Parity-Check (qLDPC) codes that achieve optimal performance while satisfying strict hardware constraints.

**Main result.** The developed multi-agent framework successfully discovers several high-performing, structurally distinct qLDPC code candidates with competitive rate-distance trade-offs for various weight classes.

**Method.** A novel multi-agent AI framework is employed in a closed loop to search the space of coset-orbit balanced-product codes, optimizing performance metrics against practical constraints like block length and overall weight.

**Model / system.** The work focuses on quantum error correction using qLDPC codes. These codes encode logical qubits by distributing information across physical qubits via sparse parity checks, which are constructed using specific algebraic structures derived from finite groups.

**Key observables.** Code parameters $[[n, k, d]]$ (block length, encoded qubits, distance), the rate ($k/n$), and a composite performance metric $Q = k d^2 / n$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Constraints include binary CSS codes with block length $n \le 400$ and overall weight $w \le 10$. Performance is evaluated under code-capacity depolarizing noise.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The search relies on the assumption that structured agentic AI can efficiently explore complex combinatorial spaces, and performance evaluation uses established decoding protocols (BP-OSD) and distance estimation techniques (QDistEvol).

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the multi-agent discovery framework loop. Figure 2 organizes comparative results for discovered codes across different overall-weight classes ($w$).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem, details the multi-agent search methodology (combining proposal/review loops), presents the construction space (coset-orbit balanced-product codes), reports key findings with specific code examples and performance metrics, and concludes by validating the approach's utility for hardware design.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can encode multiple logical qubits using sparse parity checks, yet searching for useful finite-length instances remains a challenging design problem because code performance must be optimized while satisfying practical constraints. Motivated by recent advances in artificial-intelligence agents for scientific discovery, we develop a multi-agent framework for discovering practical qLDPC codes. The framework combines specialist proposal and review, persistent scientific memory, long-horizon evolution of executable programs, and deterministic construction and evaluation within a closed-loop search. These programs instantiate coset-orbit balanced-product codes, providing a search space that includes bicycle and lifted-product constructions as well as non-normal subgroup actions. To incorporate practical constraints, we restrict the search to binary CSS codes with block length $n\leq400$ and overall weight $w\leq10$. Within this regime, the framework discovers codes with leading or competitive rate--distance performance in every weight class considered, with representative instances including $[[288,16,18]]$ at $w=7$, $[[288,18,18]]$ at $w=9$, and $[[234,28,18]]$ at $w=10$. The search also uncovers structurally distinct, high-performing constructions, including a $[[336,12,\leq24]]$ candidate and a $[[368,18,16]]$ code, both of which are genuine balanced-product constructions with non-normal subgroup actions. When evaluated under code-capacity depolarizing noise using a common BP-OSD decoding protocol, the discovered codes also exhibit low logical failure rates. Together, these results provide hardware-relevant finite-length candidates for further experimental evaluation and show how structured agentic search can contribute to scientific discovery.

</details>
